activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: The United Kingdom's standard rate of VAT, a sales tax built into most prices, has been 20 percent since January 4, 2011.
story:
Alexandre turned his first paycheque over twice, as though the reverse might carry an apology. He had been hired at the garden centre three weeks ago, forty hours a week at minimum wage, and he had done the arithmetic on the bus every night: hours times rate, a number he had guarded like a secret. The number on the cheque was smaller by almost a fifth. He sat in the business classroom before the bell, the paycheque flattened under his palm, and decided that someone, somewhere, had made a mistake and that he was going to prove it.

Khloe dropped into the seat beside him with a printed page and a problem of her own. "Look at this," she said. It was a receipt from a bookshop in London, sent by her cousin, along with a photograph of the shop itself because Khloe was saving for a trip and wanted to know exactly what things cost there. "I'm building a budget. But the receipt's broken." She pointed at the total, £24.00, and then at the empty space below it. "There's no tax line anywhere. Do they not charge tax in England? Because if so, my whole plan changes."

"There's always tax," Alexandre said, with more certainty than he felt. In Canada the tax lines eviscerated a receipt's tidy total, GST and provincial sales tax stacked at the bottom like a verdict. He pulled out his own examples: a coffee receipt from the cafeteria, thirteen percent added at the till, and his paycheque stub with its columns, income tax, EI, CPP, each deduction listed with bureaucratic calm as if it were doing him a favour. "Everything gets taxed. Yours is just missing a line."

Ms. Weber started the lesson, something about gross and net income, and Alexandre only half listened because he was still doing subtraction on his stub. He had expected the deductions to be small. They were not small. His father had an aphorism about this, delivered every April with a sardonic lift of the eyebrow: the government shakes your hand and counts your fingers. Alexandre had always laughed at it. Now he counted his own fingers and found the joke less funny, though he wasn't ready to admit the old man had been right about anything.

Khloe passed him a folded note partway through class, which was her way of arguing without getting caught. "If the books are taxed," she had written, "then the cousin overpaid or the shop cheated. Either way my budget is wrong. Check it for me." Beneath that she'd copied the receipt's details in her narrow print: one book, £20.00; total, £24.00. Alexandre looked at those two numbers for a long moment. Twenty, twenty-four. He knew that gap. It was the same shape as the gap on his paycheque, the one he'd been treating as a mistake all morning, and something in his chest went quiet and careful, the way it did before a test he hadn't studied for.

He raised his hand. "Ms. Weber, on a UK receipt, where's the tax?" She smiled the smile of a teacher who had planted something weeks ago and said only, "What do you notice about the total?" That was all, and it was enough. Alexandre bent over the note, pencil moving. If the book was £20 and the total was £24, then four pounds had been added, and four was a fifth of twenty. He wrote 20% and sat back, hearing his own pulse. He looked up the detail on his phone under the desk, careful, thumbs slow, and found it: the UK's sales tax, called VAT, built into the price, had stood at 20 percent since January 4, 2011. Not missing. Hidden in plain sight, the way his own deductions were hidden inside the number he'd been guarding on the bus. Nobody had stolen from him. The system just didn't advertise itself.

He wrote back to Khloe on the same note: "Your receipt isn't broken. The tax is already inside the price, twenty percent, and it's been that rate since January 2011. Your budget's fine, but everything there costs more than the sticker says, more than you think it does." He hesitated, then added, "Same as my paycheque. I did the math wrong the whole time." He slid the note across and watched her read it, watched her mouth form the word VAT silently, watched her frown and then, slowly, nod. Her trip would cost more than her budget said. She underlined one line in her notebook and started revising.

After the bell Alexandre stayed behind a minute, stub still on the desk. He wasn't sure which he resented more, the losing or the not having known, and he suspected those were two different complaints that would take a long time to separate. He folded the paycheque and put it in his back pocket. Khloe leaned in at the door. "Still coming Friday?" she asked, pen behind her ear, notebook against her chest. "I'm going to reprice the whole list tonight." He picked up his bag. "Only if you buy the coffee," he said. "I've seen what they do to a total."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross introduced the five stages of denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance in her 1969 book On Death and Dying, originally to describe terminally ill patients facing their own death.
story:
Sara stood at the sink with her grandfather's coffee cup, the one with the hairline crack down its side that he had refused to throw away, and tried to decide whether washing it counted as keeping something or letting it go. The kitchen smelled of the casseroles neighbours had been leaving on the porch since Tuesday, when her mother had come home from the hospital with her coat still buttoned and sat down at the table without taking off her shoes. Sara had washed this cup twice already this week. She turned it under the tap a third time.

Her mother was at the funeral home now with an aunt, and Sara had been given one job, which was to find the photo they wanted for the order of service: Grandfather in the orchard, 1974. She had the shoebox open on the table, the good tablecloth pushed aside, and she was sorting photographs with the somnolence of someone who had slept four hours a night since it happened, moving slowly, misreading dates, setting aside pictures of strangers who turned out to be herself.

The problem, the one she could not say out loud to anyone, was that she did not feel anything that matched the list. In health class in the spring, Ms. Dang had put the five stages on the board, denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance, and had said it like a train route with stations, and Sara had copied it into her notebook and underlined it twice. She had been waiting at one of the stations for six days now. Instead she felt hungry at odd times and had laughed at a meme on Thursday and then felt like a criminal for laughing, and none of that was on the board.

She texted Simona, who answered from the lake where her family was still camping: "my grandma cried for like a month straight so maybe you're on depression but the quiet kind?" Sara typed "maybe" and put the phone face down on the table. Atticus sent a link to a grief website with the same five words in a diamond chart, as though a different shape would make her recognize herself in it. She closed it. She found the orchard photograph, finally, wedged between two recipes in Grandfather's handwriting, and set it on the counter where she could see it while she thought.

Ms. Dang lived three doors down, and when Sara went to return the casserole dish she had been sent with, the door opened onto a smell of cardamom and a hallway stacked with books. Ms. Dang asked about the photograph, and Sara, surprising herself, asked instead whether the stages were true. Ms. Dang said she didn't teach it as gospel anymore, and then went to a shelf and pulled down a book with a cracked spine, On Death and Dying, published in 1969, and said the author's name was Elisabeth Kübler-Ross, and said, "She wrote it about her own terminally ill patients, facing their own deaths. Not about the people left behind."

Sara took the book home and read the introduction standing at the counter, still in her jacket. The patients, the dying ones, were the ones the stages were written for. Somewhere along the way everyone had picked it up and carried it over to the mourners, the ones at the kitchen table with a cracked cup, and it fit them badly and they blamed themselves for the fit. She felt something loosen, though she was careful not to call it relief, because relief would mean she was glad, and she was not glad about anything connected to this week.

She still thought the list was not worthless. Grandmother, in the hospital corridor, had said "if we had caught it a week earlier," which was bargaining if anything was, and one of the aunts had been furious at the cardiologist in a way that had frightened Sara until she understood it was not really about the cardiologist. So the map was real for some people, some of the time, and useless as a schedule, and Sara held both of those in her head at once the way you hold a cup that is hot on one side. She could not yet say which her own grief would turn out to be, or whether it would be legible at all, and she decided she was allowed not to know.

Her mother came home near dark with the proofs for the order of service and a bag of groceries nobody had asked for, a munificent amount of food for three people, as if abundance could be made to stand in for something. Sara put the orchard photograph on top of the stack. "Found it," she said. "It was with his recipes." Her mother picked it up, held it close to the window light, and put it back down without a word. Sara filled the kettle, set Grandfather's cup beside her own, and turned on the burner.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: Putting another writer's idea into your own words still requires a citation, because plagiarism covers using ideas without credit, not only copying exact wording.
story:
Mr. Kowalski set the stack of style guides on the front desk and said the papers were due in three weeks, footnotes and bibliography included, and that the argument had to be Landon's own. Landon had chosen the Auburn dam controversy, mostly because his grandfather had worked on it, and partly because nobody else in the class would pick something so boring it felt safe. By Thursday he had nine sources photocopied and spread across his bed like evidence at a trial no one was attending.

The problem arrived with Lachlan, who leaned across the aisle in the library and slid his laptop toward Landon. "Check this," Lachlan said. His paragraph on flood control was clean, confident, unfootnoted. "I rewrote it completely. Not a single word the same. That's fine, right? You only cite when you copy."

Landon looked at the screen. He recognized the shape of the ideas even if he didn't recognize the sentences, because he had read the same article two nights earlier, the one by the hydrologist with the long argument about sediment. Lachlan had squeezed the meaning through different words, but the skeleton underneath was somebody else's skeleton. He said, "I don't think it works like that."

"It's in my own words," Lachlan said. "That's the whole point of putting it in your own words."

Something about that bothered Landon, and he couldn't immediately say what, which was the kind of thing that kept him up. He spent his study hall reading the style guide Mr. Kowalski had handed out, the section on academic honesty, and there it was in the middle of a page about quoting: a line stating that plagiarism covers using ideas without credit, not only copying exact wording, and that rewording a source still requires a citation. He read it twice, then copied it onto his palm with a pen because his notebook was in his locker.

At lunch he found Lachlan at the long table near the vending machines, next to Roger, who was trying to extrude a stuck bag of chips from the coil with two fingers and losing. "I found it," Landon said, showing his palm. "It's the ideas too. If you use somebody's idea, you cite it even if you change every word."

Lachlan took Landon's hand and read it, frowning. "So paraphrasing doesn't get you out of it."

"Paraphrasing is just the packaging," Landon said. "The idea still belongs to the hydrologist. You'd put his name in a footnote either way."

Roger abandoned the vending machine and looked over. "So what's the point of paraphrasing at all?"

Landon considered this while Roger finally wrenched the chips free and split them three ways, an act of recompense for the twenty minutes he'd spent failing. "The point is your paper reads like a person wrote it," Landon said slowly, "and the footnote is you being honest about where the thinking came from. I guess those aren't opposites. You do both at once."

That night he sat with his own draft and found the problem waiting for him too, patient and familiar. He had written three sentences about sediment buildup that were genuinely his phrasing, but the observation itself came from the hydrologist, and from his grandfather before that, in a different vocabulary, over dinner years ago. He added a footnote. Then, two paragraphs later, he found a sentence he couldn't source at all, something about the river having its own schedule, and he left it unfootnoted and felt strange about it, because he couldn't prove it was his. Maybe everything he thought was his own was just something he'd absorbed without noticing the transfer. He wrote the bibliography in the style the guide required, alphabetical, hanging indents, and noticed that a proper bibliography had a kind of honesty to it, a public list of debts.

The morning the papers were due, Mr. Kowalski collected them at the door without ceremony. Lachlan handed his over with a full page of footnotes, more than he'd ever written before. "Took me until midnight," he said. Roger turned in his paper on stadium funding and then leaned toward the window, where the parking lot was filling with light.

Landon stood in line behind them holding his pages, and when his turn came he noticed his hands had ink on them, the copied rule still half legible across his palm, faded to a ghost of blue. Mr. Kowalski took the paper and said, "Auburn. Ambitious." Landon looked down at his hand, then back up. "I cited everything," he said. "I think."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: A 1985 study by Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky called basketball's 'hot hand' an illusion, but a 2018 reanalysis by Miller and Sanjurjo found a statistical flaw and evidence of streak shooting.
story:
The arena smelled like cold rubber and burnt coffee, and Kaylee had the middle seat, wedged between her father and Malaya, with Benny leaning over the rail from the row behind. The Wolves were down two with eight minutes left in the third period, and their winger, number 17, had just scored his second goal in four shifts. The scoreboard camera found him on the bench, jaw working, not celebrating.

"That's it, he's hot," her father said, standing halfway out of his seat. "Feed him the puck every shift. That's the whole game right there."

"He scored two," Benny said. "Two is not hot, two is Tuesday."

Kaylee's father turned around slowly, with the gravitas of a man who had been watching hockey since before any of them were born. "You don't coach by spreadsheet, kid. You coach by what you see."

Kaylee had heard this argument before, at dinner, in the car, over the dishwasher. For years she had taken her father's side without thinking, the way you take a side you're assigned at birth. Then last semester Ms. Ito had handed her a photocopied paper for an extra-credit writeup, and the side she'd been standing on had gotten complicated. She had the photocopied pages in her bag right now, actually, because she'd been reading them on the bus, which was a very Kaylee thing to have done.

"He's not crazy," she said, and her father looked at her like she'd switched jerseys. "I mean, the hot hand thing. There was this study in 1985, Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky, they looked at basketball shooters and called the hot hand an illusion. Everybody believed in streaks and the numbers said no."

"Thank you," Benny said, spreading his hands like a lawyer resting his case.

"I'm not done," Kaylee said. The Wolves' center won the faceoff and number 17 carried the puck up the boards, and the whole section rose, and nothing came of it, and they all sat back down. "In 2018, Miller and Sanjurjo reanalyzed it. They found a statistical flaw in the original study. And evidence of streak shooting. So the hot hand might be real, some."

Her father tapped the brim of his cap down, the way he did when he was deciding whether to be pleased. "So what you're telling me is, I'm right, and science took thirty years to catch up."

"That's not what I'm telling you." Number 17 went out for his next shift and took a weak shot from a bad angle, and the goalie swallowed it. Benny made a low ooooh sound. Kaylee kept her eyes on the play. "What I'm telling you is that both things can be true. Sometimes a guy's really streaking, and sometimes we just see a pattern because two goals in four minutes feels like a fire. The hard part is you can't always tell which one is happening while it's happening."

Malaya, who had been quiet through all of this, working through a small paper boat of nachos, said, "So you're saying nobody knows anything."

"I'm saying I don't know this," Kaylee said. "The 2018 people found real evidence and they also found a flaw in how everyone had been counting. So believing in the hot hand isn't dumb anymore, but disbelieving it used to be the smart position. Both of those were honest. It's the certainty that's the problem."

Her father said nothing for a whole shift. She knew what he was doing; he was deciding whether to argue with her or be proud of her, and she also knew that with him those often looked identical from the outside. Two seasons ago she had quit her own team, mid-year, and he had spent a month barely speaking to her, and they had never once said the word quit out loud in the same room. She had told herself then that she left because the coach vilified every mistake, made errors into character flaws, and maybe that was even true. But standing in this cold air next to him, she suspected she had also left because she couldn't stand being watched by someone who believed so completely in what he saw.

"There's a minute forty left," Malaya said. "If he scores again, you owe me a milkshake, and if he doesn't, I owe you."

"That's a terrible bet," Kaylee said. "That's a sample size of one."

"Then don't take it, cerebral." Malaya held out her pinky.

The Wolves pulled their goalie with fifty seconds left. The puck came loose at the point, and number 17 picked it up with empty net in front of him, and the whole arena got to its feet at once, and Kaylee found she had laced her pinky through Malaya's without deciding to. He was flying down the ice, alone, and her father was shouting, and she was shouting too, and she did not know yet what she believed about what would happen next. He shot.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Research by linguist Paul Nation and colleagues suggests readers need to know about 98 percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help.
story:
On Tuesday afternoon the language room smelled of whiteboard marker and someone's microwaved soup, and Natalie sat with a news article in German that she had chosen precisely because it looked impressive. It concerned, as far as she could tell, either a flood or a debate about a flood, possibly both, and every paragraph was a locked door. She had circled eleven words in the first three lines alone. Grayden leaned across the aisle and peered at the carnage.

"You've circled half the page," he said. "Is that a reading strategy or a cry for help?"

"It's annotation," Natalie said, with dignity, and circled a twelfth word, "Verantwortung," which she suspected meant responsibility but which might just as easily have meant a type of sausage.

Mr. Otieno moved between the desks with his hands clasped behind his back like a man touring an exhibition of struggling. "By Friday," he reminded them, "one article, read, and summarised aloud to a partner. Not read aloud. Summarised. In the language." He said this every year and every year it produced the same communal groan, which he appeared to enjoy the way a farmer enjoys rain.

Jonas, two rows over, was already finished. He had chosen an article about a cat stuck in a subterranean parking garage, rescued by firefighters, beloved by a nation, and he had clearly understood every word of it, because he kept grinning at his paper and occasionally saying "die Feuerwehr" to no one. Natalie regarded him the way one regards a person who has found the escalator while one is still climbing the stairs. She turned back to her flood-or-debate. She looked up "Verantwortung." It meant responsibility. No sausage. Small mercies.

That evening she did the thing she swore she would not do, which was go looking for a reason her brain felt like a wrung-out dish towel. She typed "why is reading so hard in a foreign language" into the search bar, braced for internet nonsense, and instead found herself in a university page about vocabulary research. She read it twice. A linguist named Paul Nation, it said, and colleagues, had found that readers need to know about ninety-eight percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help. She sat very still, as if the fact might startle and flee.

She counted. Her article had roughly two hundred and forty words, and she confidently knew perhaps a hundred and forty of them, which was not ninety-eight percent of anything except a disaster. To read it comfortably she would have needed to be unfamiliar with fewer than five words total. Five. She had circled twelve before lunch. It was not that she was bad at this. It was arithmetic. She felt absurdly absolved, as though a judge had rapped a gavel and declared her innocent of laziness, and then she felt the gavel swing back, because knowing the math did not change it. She still wanted the impressive article. She wanted to stand up on Friday and summarize something about responsibility, even if it had turned out not to be a sausage.

On Wednesday she brought the printout of a different piece, a short item about a bicycle lane in a small town, which Grayden pronounced "aggressively boring" and which Natalie pronounced "at my level," and then, before he could tease her further, "which is a real place that exists, unlike my flood." She explained the ninety-eight percent thing while jabbing her pencil at her counts, and Jonas drifted over, trailed by the ghost of his cat article, nodding like a small smug acolyte of easy texts.

"So the trick," Grayden said slowly, "is to pick something where you only don't know like four words. That feels illegal."

"It feels like homework," Natalie said. "It's supposed to feel like that."

By Friday she could summarize the bicycle lane piece aloud, haltingly, with her hands conducting invisible traffic, and Mr. Otieno listened with his eyebrows in a state of cautious approval. Jonas, her assigned partner, asked her in German whether the town was happy about the lane. She understood the question entirely, every single word of it, and the pleasure of that was ridiculous, disproportionate, like being proud of a doorknob. "Ich glaube ja," she said. I think so. Then, because the flood article still sat folded in her bag like a dare, she pulled it out and laid it beside the bicycle lane one, the two of them side by side, and counted the circles still left on the hard page, out loud, all twelve.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: In his Poetics, Aristotle said a well-made plot is a whole with a beginning, a middle and an end.
story:
Ethan had the whole garage apartment of his grandmother's house to himself for the week, which was the problem, because the notebook was still blank on page one. The assignment from Ms. Navarro's summer workshop was due in six days: a ten-minute play drawn from a moment in his own life, staged in the church basement with two other students as actors. He had chosen the easy memory, the fight the spring his father didn't come to his regional semifinal, and he had written four pages of two people yelling in a kitchen before the dialogue simply stopped. There was no more to say. He knew what had happened afterward; he just couldn't make it into anything.

His grandmother's house sat above the reservoir where the plains broke into montane forest, blue firs climbing the ridge behind the garden, and she kept the window over her desk aimed at that slope as if the view were furniture. Ethan sat there on Tuesday morning with the notebook open, and she put a cup of tea beside him without asking whether he wanted it. "You look like your grandfather before a sermon," she said. "He'd pace the hallway muttering at the ceiling."

"I'm supposed to write a play," Ethan said. "It's about a real thing. But it keeps ending in the middle."

She was gone longer than it took to fetch tea. When she came back she carried a paperbound book with a cracked spine, her copy from a community college class she'd taken in her forties, and dropped it on the desk. "Start at the marked page. I'm going to weed the beans." She did not offer to discuss it, which he understood was her way of respecting him, though at seventeen it also felt like being handed a rope in the dark.

The marked page was Aristotle. In his Poetics, Aristotle said a well-made plot is a whole with a beginning, a middle and an end. Ethan read the sentence three times. It was so obvious it was almost insulting, and yet his four pages were all middle, a kitchen, an argument, a door left open, and then nothing. The play had a beginning and a middle, but the moment everything was waiting for, the moment something changed, he had never written, possibly because he had never found it in life either. He had walked out of that kitchen eighteen months ago and nobody had ever said what came next. He transfix himself on the sentence, pencil under it, and the firs on the ridge went dark as a cloud crossed, then bright again.

That afternoon Mackenna biked over, helmet still buckled, because he'd texted her that the play was dying. She read the four pages in the lawn chairs while he pretended to pick raspberries he had no intention of picking. "This is good," she said, which he didn't believe. "But it stops."

"I know."

"So what changed? Between the door and now. Something must have."

He started to say nothing, and the honest version came out instead: he didn't know whether anything had. His father had shown up to the consolation match, unasked, and they'd said maybe forty words all day, and won, and driven home with the radio on, and it had felt like repair without ever being named as repair. Mackenna frowned at the page. "Then that's the play. Not the fight. The day after, where nobody says anything and it still counts."

The problem was that nothing happened, and the solution, which he worked out alone that evening while his grandmother cooked and the montane dark came down, was that nothing happening had to be staged as an event. He wrote a scene in bleachers. A father arrives late, stands apart, sits when there's a seat. A son scores and does not look over, then looks over once. On the drive home the radio plays and the father's hand rests on the gearshift near the son's knee. Two actors, one bench, a steering wheel suggested by a chair. It was a whole. It began when the father walked in, it middle-ed through the silence, and it ended with the engine cut in the driveway and neither of them moving yet, which was not resolution but was, at least, an end.

The staging on Friday nearly foundered on Ariana, who was playing the father and wanted to add a reconciliation speech in the car, because silence, she argued, read as an accident rather than a choice. "If I just sit there, people will think we forgot the ending." Ethan told her the sitting was the ending, and she looked at him for a long second and then took her mark. There was also the small disincentive that his own father had been invited, by his grandmother, without consulting him, and was in the third row, which made the gearshift business either the bravest or the most reckless thing Ethan had ever done. He decided not to decide which.

The lights came up on the bench. Ariana walked in late, stood, sat. Mackenna, in the son's role, scored without looking over, then looked over once, and in the church basement you could hear the air conditioner and nothing else, and nobody coughed. When the engine cut and neither of them moved, the audience held its breath as if the play might still do something, and then Ethan let it go to black. In the third row his father's hands were folded, and in the lobby afterward he said, "Your grandmother ever tell you she got an A in that class?" and Ethan said no, and his father said, "Ask her about the ending of her final paper sometime," and put on his jacket.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: A 2018 replication by Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan found the link between waiting and later achievement was much smaller, and shrank further after accounting for family background.
story:
The chicken was dry and Nicolas's grandfather had reached the part of dinner he liked best, the part where the table became an audience. He had done this at every family meal since Nicolas could remember: fork down, napkin smoothed across one knee, and then some principle of life delivered as though he had coined it that afternoon. Tonight it was patience.

"You know about the marshmallow test," the grandfather said. It was not a question. "Children, one marshmallow, and if they can wait, they get a second one. The ones who waited did better later. In school, in everything. Character, Nicolas. That's what it measures." He picked up his fork again, having apparently settled the matter, and Nicholas's mother gave the potatoes a quarter turn in their dish, her way of signaling neutrality.

Nicolas pushed a piece of chicken to the edge of his plate. He had written a paper on exactly this in Mr. Joseph's class last spring, and Mr. Joseph, who had a habit of handing back essays with a single comment scrawled at the bottom, had written one word on his: good. The paper had been about a 2018 replication by Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan. Nicolas had read it twice, partly because Addisyn had found it and sent it to him with the message "your grandfather's favorite argument," and partly because he had suspected, correctly, that it would be useful ammunition someday.

"It's more complicated than that," Nicolas said. His grandfather raised an eyebrow, an incipient smile suggesting he was prepared to be amused by whatever came next. "They ran it again in 2018. Watts, Duncan and Quan. Ten times more kids than the original, a more representative sample. And the link between waiting and later achievement was much smaller than the first study found. After they accounted for family background, it shrank further." He heard his own voice go flat, essay-voice, and tried to soften it. "The kids who waited did a little better. A little. Not the dramatic thing everybody remembers."

His grandfather chewed for a while. Across the table, Nicolas's sister, who was fourteen and wanted, above all else in this world, to be exempt from family dinners, was suddenly interested. She had a marshmallow in the pantry, Nicolas knew, kept there for exactly the kind of hot chocolate emergency she considered a monthly occurrence.

"So patience is worthless," the grandfather said.

"That's not what it says either." Nicolas was aware of the trap: his grandfather wanted to impute to him a whole philosophy, some careless adolescent nihilism, and if Nicolas let him, the argument would be about that instead of about the study. "It says waiting might be a symptom of something else, not the cause. Kids from steadier households could afford to wait. The marshmallow wasn't building their future. It was reporting on their present."

The sister spoke for the first time since the salad. "So if I eat my marshmallow now, I'm just, what, being honest about my circumstances?" She was already half out of her chair.

"Sit," their mother said.

Nicolas thought about Felix, who had waited for nothing in his life, who had applied to one college, early, absurdly, and gotten in, and who was now going to Montreal in September while Nicolas was still weighing two offers against each other like a jeweler with a fake scale. There was a version of this where Felix's impulsiveness had simply been a good bet, and a version where Nicolas's deliberation was the only thing that had kept three bad options from becoming four. He could not prove which version was true. That was the part his essay had ended on, and the part Mr. Joseph's "good" had seemed, Nicolas thought, to actually endorse. The pragmatics of waiting mattered: what you were waiting for, who had put the marshmallow in front of you, what else was in the cupboard.

"I still say you should take the scholarship," his grandfather said, which was the real subject, the one the marshmallow had been parading as. "State school, money in the bank, done. That's what a person who waits does."

"Or it's what a person who's scared does," Nicolas said. "The study can't tell those apart. That's kind of the whole point." He reached for the potatoes his mother had been guarding with her spoon, and she served him without comment, a small treaty signed in starch.

The sister, meanwhile, had returned from the pantry with the marshmallow and set it in the center of the table like evidence. She looked at their grandfather, then at Nicolas.

"One," she said. "No second one coming. Your move."

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: The 'guidance hypothesis' from motor learning research holds that feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it, so less frequent feedback often helps retention.
story:
Mr. Novák put the whistle around Tristan's neck on the first cold Tuesday of the season and said the under-twelves were his for forty minutes. Tristan had expected to hand out cones. Instead he inherited twelve small players whose passes, in Saturday's match, had gone everywhere except to a teammate, and a coach who stood behind him calling a correction after every ball. Tuck your plant foot. Open your hips. Look up first. By the end of practice the youngest boy, a defender named only by his shouts for the ball, was passing to nobody and staring at the sideline before the ball had even left his foot.

"They only look good when he's talking," Tristan told Iman at lunch, sketching cones on the back of his chemistry notes. Iman had broken his ankle in the fall and could not play, which was its own small disaster, but he had appointed himself Tristan's analyst anyway. "It's like they can't do it alone." Tristan had spent the previous night in a reverie of coaching manuals, half asleep over his laptop, and one phrase had surfaced again and again: the guidance hypothesis. Iman had read it over his shoulder and said, "That's it, that's the whole thing. Feedback after every single attempt makes them dependent on it. Less frequent feedback helps retention." He said it the way he reported injuries, flat and certain, and Tristan wrote it on his hand.

The next practice, Tristan ran the plan he had built for their real weakness, which was not passing itself but passing under movement: a diamond drill, ten yards to a partner who never stood still. When Mr. Novák began his patter, Tristan lifted a hand and asked if he could try something. He would say nothing unless a player asked, and even then only every so often, and otherwise he would hold his tongue and let the mistakes happen. Mr. Novák looked at him for a long moment, the whistle slack in his fingers, and then walked to the far side of the grid and stood with his arms folded, which felt seismic at the time, though nothing in the world had actually moved.

The first ten minutes were agony. Balls rolled out of bounds. Raphael, the smallest kid and the loudest, turned around after every bad pass with his chin already braced for the correction that did not come. Tristan counted attempts in his head. After the fifth, he said one thing, quietly, to the whole group: "Watch where your partner is running, not where he is." Then silence again. Somewhere around the twentieth attempt, the passes stopped dying in the grass between players. Raphael, waiting for a ball at the far cone, stopped checking Tristan's face and started checking the runner instead.

That night Iman sent him a message, long and typed fast: "Don't take me off this. I know I can't play till spring and everyone's being weird about it, like I'm made of glass. But I watched every game from the bench and I know which kid rushes and which kid waits. I want to come Tuesday and call the drill from the sideline while you coach. Also bring the good pinnies, the blue ones, the red ones make Kai look like a traffic cone." Tristan read it twice, then a third time, and understood that the ankle had not been the only thing Iman was carrying around all winter.

On Tuesday they ran it together. Iman sat on a folded chair at midfield with his boot propped on a ball, calling patterns, and Tristan moved through the diamonds saying almost nothing. When a boy named for a grandfather nobody could pronounce kept missing the diagonal ball, Tristan let four misses go by, felt the old itch to fix it, subjugated the itch on purpose, and only then said, "Try it earlier, before he's covered." The fifth attempt arced perfectly into the runner's stride, and the boy did not look to the sideline at all. He just did it again.

Saturday, Mr. Novák stood ten yards behind Tristan with the whistle in his pocket and said nothing for the whole first half. The under-twelves lost two to one. Their passing, though, held together without a single voice behind them, and the youngest defender, unmarked in the final minute, lifted his head, saw the run, and played the ball into space that arrived exactly when Raphael did.

After the final whistle, Tristan and Iman stood at the touchline while the kids collected cones. Mr. Novák came over, held out his hand for the whistle, and then, instead of taking it, closed Tristan's fingers back around it. "Tuesday," he said, and walked off toward the parking lot. Iman leaned on his shoulder, grinning at the sky, and Raphael ran past them chasing a runaway ball into the far goal net.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: ProPublica, founded in 2007 as a nonprofit newsroom funded by donations, became the first online news source to win a Pulitzer Prize, in 2010.
story:
The group chat had been named "Oracle Staff (OFFICIAL)" by Karlee back in September, when nobody had thought to remonstrate about the capital letters or the word official, and by now the name had hardened into fact. Aaron lay on his bed with the phone above his face, watching the typing bubble appear and disappear while Karlee composed whatever she was composing about the newspaper's money problem.

"Here's the thing," she finally posted, in three separate messages the way she always did. "Bell's Pharmacy wants to buy a back page ad. Full price. That covers printing for two months."

Ariella replied within a minute. She was the features editor and had opinions about everything, most of them good. "Bell's is the place that reported Marisol for shopkeeping when she was fourteen. We take their money, we can never write about them. Or about Main Street rents, because Bell's is a landlord."

Aaron typed, deleted, typed again. "We can't write about Main Street anyway. We don't have the budget to do actual reporting. That's the whole problem."

It was true in a way that annoyed everyone. The Oracle ran event recaps and cafeteria polls and a column Ariella wrote called "Sights and Signs" that Mr. Park, the adviser, privately called the best thing in the paper. Real stories required bus fare and time and the freedom to burn both on something that might not pan out. The school district gave them nothing beyond a room and the ancient iMacs. Whatever independence the paper had, it had bought with bake sales and, now, possibly with Bell's Pharmacy.

Karlee sent a screenshot of a spreadsheet she'd built at midnight, columns in descending shades of green. "Ads: predictable. Donations: not. We ask for donations, we get whatever people feel like giving, and we plan nothing."

Ariella: "We ask for ads, we get exactly what advertisers feel like letting us write. Predictable in the other direction."

Aaron sat up. The ceiling above his bed had a water stain shaped like a fist, and he had spent enough evenings staring at it that it had become a kind of oratory, a place he went to argue with himself. He typed: "Wait. There are newsrooms that run on donations. Not ads. Like ProPublica." He paused. "I read about it for Mr. Park's class. It was founded in 2007 as a nonprofit newsroom funded by donations, and in 2010 it became the first online news source to win a Pulitzer Prize."

Karlee: "the WHAT prize"

Ariella: "Pulitzer. The big journalism one. Aaron are you serious"

"Serious," he typed. "Look it up." He heard, from downstairs, his mother remonstrating gently with the oven, which had been running cold since November, and the sound was oddly steadying, a small domestic argument with a clear outcome. He added, "So it's not just a theory. It's been done, and it worked at a level nobody thought an online-only place could reach."

Karlee was quiet for four minutes, an eternity. Then: "ok but ProPublica is for grown-ups with rich friends. Who donates to us. Parents who want to feel good?"

"Parents who want a paper that isn't a recital of the winter concert," Ariella wrote. "There's a difference between taking money from a business you might cover and taking twenty dollars from somebody's mom."

"Both of them want something," Karlee answered. "Moms want their kid's name in print. That's not nothing."

Aaron got up and walked to the window. Across the street, the light in Mr. Park's kitchen was on; Mr. Park was grading, or reading, or eating some epicurean leftover at ten at night, which was his habit, and Aaron felt the odd comfort of knowing an adult's life in its small specifics. He thought about the difference Karlee kept circling. An advertiser buys a relationship. A donor makes a gift, and the gift could curdle into expectation too, but there was no contract, no page reserved, nothing to lose if you published something unwelcome. Or maybe there was, just a softer one. He couldn't make that part resolve, and he suspected nobody could, that every way of funding a paper came with a hand on it somewhere.

He typed slowly. "Here's what I think. We ask for donations from families and alumni. Small ones, so no single person feels owed. If it doesn't cover printing, then we talk about ads, but we put a rule in the bylaws that we never run an ad from a business in a story we're actively covering. And we say the rule out loud in the paper itself, so readers know."

Ariella: "That's actually a constitution."

Karlee: "that's actually WORK. who writes the bylaws"

"You do," Aaron typed. "You love spreadsheets. Bylaws are spreadsheets with sentences."

There was a pause, then a single crying-laughing emoji from Karlee, then, "fine. meeting thursday at lunch. someone tell park."

"He's across the street from me," Aaron wrote. "I'll go knock."

He pulled on a hoodie over his T-shirt and went down the stairs, past the kitchen where his mother stood with her hand flat on the oven door, testing it like a doctor checking a pulse. "Tell Mr. Park the heating element's shot," she said, not looking up. "He'll know a guy."

The night air was colder than the hallway had let on. Mr. Park's porch light came on before Aaron even reached the steps, and the door opened on the smell of something with garlic in it.

"We're switching to donations," Aaron said. "ProPublica won a Pulitzer before anybody thought an online newsroom could. Thursday at lunch, Karlee's writing bylaws, and we need you to pretend you didn't already think of this."

Mr. Park leaned against the doorframe, unhurried, holding his fork loosely at his side like a man interrupted in the middle of a private ceremony. "I'll bring the good coffee," he said.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Simple interest is calculated as I = P times r times t: the principal, times the annual interest rate, times the time in years.
story:
The queue inside the bank moved at the pace of syrup, and by the time Rose reached the middle of it, the afternoon heat had begun to enervate her, so that her plan, which had felt airtight on the bus, now seemed full of holes she could poke a finger through. The deposit for the summer intensive was due by five o'clock, six hundred dollars, and in her pocket she had a letter from her uncle and a page of arithmetic she had done at the kitchen table at midnight.

In the flashback she kept returning to, her uncle sat across from her with his sleeves rolled up, tapping the letter against his knee. "Six hundred, and I'll charge you interest," he had said. "Simple interest, not that bank stuff. You'll pay me back the principal plus what it costs to borrow, over two years." Rose had nodded as though she understood, and only after he left did she get out her calculator and work it out with the formula she'd copied from the back of her math notebook: interest equals the principal times the annual rate times the time in years. Six hundred, at six percent a year, for two years. Six hundred times point oh six times two. Seventy-two dollars. The loan would cost her six hundred and seventy-two in the end.

"Six hundred and seventy-two," Solomon murmured now, reading over her shoulder in the queue. "That's not terrible."

"It's not nothing," Rose said. "That's eleven pairs of shifts at the café." She folded the page small enough to hide in her fist.

Loan was already at the counter, waiting for them, waving with the particular impatience of someone who had given up her Saturday. She had insisted on coming, on the grounds that Rose was impecunious in a way that required supervision, and that supervision required company. "Did you bring the letter from your grandmother's lawyer?" Loan asked when Rose reached her.

"No, because there is no letter from my grandmother's lawyer. There's a rumour of a letter. My mother said the bank would know. That's the whole reason we're here."

What her mother had actually said, on the phone this morning, her voice careful and strange, was that Ms. Costa had mentioned something when they met at the shops. Ms. Costa, who had lived beside Grandmother for thirty years. Ms. Costa, who had driven her to the bank every month for the last two years of her life. Something about an account, her mother had said, and then the bus had come and Rose had missed whatever followed.

The teller was young and kept glancing at the clock behind her, which Rose chose not to interpret. "I need to know if there's an account under Eileen Marsh," Rose said, giving her grandmother's name and then, when asked, her own name and her mother's, and the date of death in June, which she had never had to say aloud to a stranger before. The teller typed, frowned slightly, typed again, and Rose felt the whole plan tilt, the six hundred and the seventy-two and the five o'clock deadline suddenly weightless, dependent on whatever appeared next on that screen.

"Sixty-two," the teller said at last, and Rose's stomach dropped before she understood. "Account sixty-two. It's a savings account. It's been accruing interest since the first deposit." She turned the monitor partway so Rose could see the balance, and Rose leaned in.

The account held eight hundred and twelve dollars. Grandmother had put in six hundred, the teller said, looking back through the records, and the rest was interest the bank had paid over two years, compounding each month. Money sitting still had grown. Money borrowed would grow the same way, only in the other direction, onto her uncle's side of the table. Rose stood there with both numbers in her head at once, the seventy-two she would owe and the two hundred and twelve nobody had owed anybody, and she could not make them sit together easily, and she did not try to.

She thought of the rectitude she had promised herself, paying her own way, owing no one; and she thought of her uncle, who had offered the loan not because he needed the interest but because he wanted her to know what borrowing felt like before the world charged her more. The clock behind the teller read twenty past four.

"One withdrawal," Rose said, sliding her ID across the counter. "Six hundred. Leave the rest in." She would tell her uncle tonight, and let him decide whether he still wanted his seventy-two dollars, and outside the glass doors Loan was already on her feet, holding up Rose's bag.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: The Islamic calendar is lunar and about 10 to 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr come roughly 10 to 11 days earlier each year.
story:
The community hall smelled like cardamom and burnt coffee, and Aidan stood at the door with his chemistry textbook under his arm, checking his phone for the third time. Exam was at nine tomorrow morning. It was already past eleven at night.

"Aidan, come sit," his mother called from the long table near the stage, where the aunties had arranged baklava in defensive formation. He sat. Across from him, Chanel was separating pistachios from a honey-drenched pastry with surgical precision, and Makayla was filming the trays for her story.

"This is the one where you can't eat all day, right?" Chanel said. "For a month?"

"Ramadan," Aidan said. "And it ended today. This is Eid."

Makayla lowered her phone. "Wait, it's in November now? Wasn't it in like, August when we were in eighth grade?"

"Freshman year it was basically summer," Chanel said. "I remember because you disappeared for a pool day."

Aidan hesitated. He'd looked it up in the library on Tuesday, after Mr. Tremblay had refused to move his makeup test and Aidan had gone hunting for an argument to bring back to him. The Islamic calendar is lunar, he'd read, and about 10 to 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr come roughly 10 to 11 days earlier each year. He'd written the numbers on his wrist like a cheat code. "It drifts," he said now. "Every year it lands ten or eleven days earlier than the last. That's why it keeps moving through the seasons."

"That's sneaky," Chanel said. "In a cool way."

"In an inconvenient way," Aidan said. "It's landing on my exam schedule."

He thought of Tuesday again, standing in Mr. Tremblay's classroom after the bell. He'd enunciated his case carefully, the way he'd practiced: that the date wasn't arbitrary, that it moved according to a real system, that a test scheduled on Eid was like scheduling one on Christmas morning. Mr. Tremblay had listened with his arms crossed, which was his listening posture and also his no posture. "I can't move a midterm for one student, Aidan." Then, softer, which was worse: "Come in before school. I'll open the room at seven."

Aidan had walked out furious. Now he wasn't sure what he'd been furious at. Not Mr. Tremblay, exactly. At the whole arrangement of things, the way two calendars could run side by side and only one of them seemed to count for exams and holidays and everything printed on the wall.

Makayla leaned across the table. "Then just leave. Study at home. Nobody's holding you hostage."

"His mother is holding him hostage," Chanel said, nodding toward the aunties.

"I heard that," his mother said, without turning around.

Somebody's little brother made off with an entire tray of dates. An uncle chased him past the basketball nets that had been pushed against the wall, and the hall collapsed into laughter, and Makayla got all of it on video. Aidan laughed too, despite himself, despite the textbook digging into his ribs like a second conscience.

Earlier in the evening, the imam had given a short talk about charity, about how the community's zakat fund had covered four families' rent this year, and Mr. Haddad, who owned the gas station on Front Street, had been thanked for being, as the imam put it, munificent beyond anyone's expectations. Mr. Haddad had turned the color of the cranberry juice. It was the only part of the night that had felt like it was about something larger than food, and Aidan had noticed that even that was practical, envelopes and receipts, a ledger passed hand to hand. Not a sermon. A system.

In school they were debating theocracy that week in civics, and a boy in the second row had argued that any state with a religious calendar was backwards by definition. Aidan had said nothing at the time. He was still turning over what he would have said, if he'd said anything. That a calendar could be a way of keeping time and also a way of keeping a people, and that these weren't the same thing as law, and that he didn't know where the line was, exactly. He didn't know. That was the honest part.

"Aidan." His mother set a plate of kebabs in front of him. "Eat. Then study in the back room if you want. Mr. Tremblay is a reasonable man."

"He's not," Aidan said. Then, "He kind of is. He's opening the school at seven for me."

"So go at seven."

Chanel raised her glass of mango juice. "To the lunar calendar. Enemy of exam schedules everywhere."

"To Eid," Makayla said. "And to Mr. Tremblay's seven a.m. keycard."

Aidan raised his glass with them and, somewhere between the toast and the first kebab, slid the textbook off his lap and onto the empty chair beside him. He'd wake at six. He'd make it work. Or he wouldn't, and he'd retake the test in January, when Eid had drifted another ten or eleven days away, deeper into whatever season came next. His mother came back with a second plate he hadn't asked for, and he ate that too.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Carryover cooking means food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a large roast's internal temperature can rise by several degrees while it rests.
story:
Elliot lit the grill at four o'clock because his father had said, for the third Sunday running, that this time he would be home to teach him the roast. The butcher's paper crackled as he unwrapped it on the folding table by the fence, and the meat sat there pale and dense, a thing that would become dinner only if he did everything right. He had the thermometer his mother used at Christmas, its probe on a long silver wire, and he had a page of notes in his own handwriting that began, in letters pressed hard enough to dent the paper, TARGET: 135.

By five the coals were white at the edges and his phone had buzzed twice. The first message was from Rian, who wanted to know if Elliot was going to Autumn's thing on Friday, and the second was from Autumn herself: Heard you're doing the roast. Don't overthink it. He texted back a photo of the grill, which felt like an answer without being one, a small subterfuge he was already tired of maintaining, since what he wanted to say was that he was terrified of ruining thirty dollars of beef on a night his father had promised to be present for.

The roast went on at 5:20. He watched the thermometer the way he watched chemistry titrations, leaning in, notebook open, and when the display read 135 he pulled the meat off with the long fork and set it on the board under foil. It was 6:15. His father was not home. Elliot texted, then called, then told himself the drive from the airport took longer on Sundays, and he stood in the backyard with the foil tented like something at a funeral.

At 6:40 he carved. The meat had gone from pink to grey across its whole middle, and it resisted the knife with a dry, shredding grain. He stood over it wondering how a thing could pass through exactly the state he'd wanted and keep going, as though the number on the display had been a promise the meat never made. He carried a plate of it to the fence, mostly to get away from it, and ate a piece standing in the grass. It tasted like an argument he'd lost.

"You cooked it to temperature and it still went grey." The voice came from the other side of the fence, and Mr. Berg appeared at the gap where a board had warped, holding his own glass of something. "Happened to me in 1988. A standing rib roast, Christmas Eve. My mother-in-law still brings it up."

"So the thermometer's wrong?"

"Thermometer's fine." Mr. Berg sipped his drink. "My daughter calls it carryover cooking. Food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat. A big roast like yours, the temperature can rise several degrees just sitting there under your foil."

Elliot looked back at the board, the grey slices, the foil crumpled beside it. Several degrees. Not the thermometer lying, but the reading being only part of the truth, a snapshot of a thing still in motion. He wondered how many other measurements worked like that, numbers that seemed final and were really just a moment in a process. "Then you pull it early," he said slowly, testing the shape of the thought.

"There's another one in your fridge," Mr. Berg said. "I watched you carry two in from the car."

Elliot had bought the backup without admitting to himself that it was a backup, because naming it would have made real, would have reified, the possibility of failing. He stood at the fence holding that knowledge, half embarrassed and half grateful, and decided not to perform gratitude. "You could have said something before the first one."

"You were doing fine. Guy's allowed one grey roast."

He went inside, retrieved the second cut of meat, and put it on the dying coals, rebuilding them with fresh charcoal while the phone in his pocket stayed dark. His mother was on shift until eleven. His father had not called. When the new thermometer reading climbed toward 128, four or five degrees below the target he'd written in his notes, Elliot lifted the roast off and let it rest under fresh foil, and he watched the display like a man watching a door he could no longer do anything about. He would not know if he'd been right until he cut into it. That was the part nobody wrote down, that even the corrected answer had to be waited for.

At 7:30 Autumn and Rian came through the side gate, uninvited and carrying bread and a bag of salad, saying his mother had texted Autumn's mother a warning that he was out here alone with a grill and his pride. Elliot lifted the foil, carved against the grain, and the centre came away rose-coloured and glossy, exactly what the first roast had refused to be. Rian stole a slice straight off the board. Mr. Berg passed two beers over the fence, one for himself and one he slid toward the table, and Elliot let it sit there unopened, still deciding. He set a plate at his father's empty place.

"Eat," said Autumn. "It's better hot."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Mexico's Day of the Dead is traditionally celebrated on November 1 and 2, when families build ofrendas, or home altars, with photos and the favorite foods and drinks of relatives who have died.
story:
The bakery box sat on the seat between Alexa and her mother, warm enough that she could feel it through her jeans. Inside was a round of pan de muerto, its crust striped with dough shaped like bones, and Alexa kept glancing at it the way you glance at a word you have copied down but not yet understood. Her grandmother had died in March, between the snow and the daffodils, and until this week Alexa had not known that her grandmother's favorite bread had a name, or that the name came with a season.

"It's called Day of the Dead," Caiden had told her in the parking lot after last period, when she'd asked why the grocery store had a whole aisle of marigolds and sugar skulls. "November first and second. My mom builds one every year. An ofrenda, like a home altar, with photos, and the person's favorite food and drinks on it. It's not spooky, it's an invitation." He had said it casually, picking at the strap of his bag, but Alexa had written the date on her palm in pen and looked at it all through the drive to practice.

Now her mother drove the long way home, past the reservoir, because the direct route went by the hospital and neither of them had said so out loud. "I called your grandmother every Sunday," her mother said, not taking her eyes off the road. "Eleven years, and I don't know what her favorite thing was to eat besides this. Isn't that something." The windshield wipers ticked twice against a spatter of rain and then stopped, as if changing their minds.

"I looked it up during study hall," Alexa said. "The whole thing. It's not till November first, so we have time." She turned the box so the twine faced her mother. "We could build the ofrenda on the dresser in the hall. The one with the mirror." Her mother was quiet through two turns, and Alexa watched her hands on the wheel, the way her thumb made small circles, an old habit that her grandmother had too. Whether grief could be inherited, or only habits, she couldn't decide.

"I was raised to believe you don't bother the dead," her mother said finally. "You pray for them and you let them rest. My mother's church inculcated that in her so deeply she flinched at Halloween." She smiled briefly, without humor. "But her mother, your great-grandmother, was from that village in the mountains. Montane country, cold at night even in summer, where the mistletoe grew on the oaks. She crossed on foot to the coast, then the isthmus, then here, and somewhere along the way we stopped doing whatever it was she did."

Alexa thought of the photograph on the mantel, the one where her great-grandmother stood squinting in a doorway with her arms crossed, looking less like a woman being remembered than a woman waiting for the rest of the family to catch up. Maybe the church and the ofrenda were not opposites. Maybe they were both ways of setting a place at a table for someone who could not come. She held the two ideas side by side the way you hold two keys, trying each in the same lock, and neither fully turned, and she was honest enough with herself to admit that.

"Mr. Thompson said something once," Alexa said. "Back when his wife died. He said the first year you don't grieve, you just take attendance. You keep noticing who's not in the room." Her mother made a small sound, half laugh, and pulled into the driveway, and the engine went quiet, and they sat for a moment with the box between them.

"Thursday," her mother said. "If we're doing this, we do it properly. Photos, the bread, a candle. We'll figure out her favorite drink. Somebody in Puebla must know, some cousin." She reached for the door handle and then stopped. "Your grandmother used to put orange peel in her coffee. I'd forgotten that until just now."

They carried the box up the steps together, and in the hall Alexa stopped in front of the dresser with the mirror and cleared the perfume bottles to one side with the flat of her hand, leaving a wide, dustless space in the middle, and set the bread down where anyone arriving could see it.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Holding static stretches for a long time, about 60 seconds or more per muscle, right before explosive activity can briefly reduce strength and power, so many programs warm up with dynamic movement.
story:
Daniel had a notebook with the days of the week printed down the left margin, and for three nights he had been filling in the boxes. Monday, hills. Tuesday, rest. Wednesday, intervals on the track. Thursday, rest. Friday, strides. Saturday, race. He liked the arithmetic of it, the way a season could be predicated on something as plain as a page of boxes, and he liked even more that nobody had asked him to do it. The coach had said only that the boys who planned their own weeks usually lasted until June.

"You're putting rest days in the middle," Danielle said, leaning over his shoulder in the bleachers, her spikes dangling from one hand. She was a sprinter, a junior, and she wanted the fourth spot on the relay more than she wanted anything she was willing to say out loud. "That looks lazy."

"That looks like a program," Daniel said.

She rolled her eyes, but she had her own notebook out a minute later, copying his margins, and he pretended not to notice.

Saturday came cold and bright, the track still glittering with yesterday's rain. Daniel had added a warm-up column to his page that morning, because a program without a warm-up felt like a house without a door. He knew one warm-up, the one his father had taught him from his own running days: find a fence, settle into a stretch, and hold it. So Daniel held each stretch the way his father had, counting slowly to sixty, sometimes past it, the hamstring trembling, the quad aching pleasantly against the rail by the start line. Then he walked to his blocks, set his feet, and waited for the gun.

The race felt wrong from the first step. He was not injured, not tired, nothing he could name. His legs simply felt flat, as though the strength had been poured out of them somewhere between the fence and the line. He ran his slowest 400 of the season, and Danielle, watching from the infield with her arms crossed, said nothing at all, which was worse than sympathy.

He did not figure it out that day. He figured it out on Monday, in the public library, because he had decided the flat feeling was a problem worth solving and he was too embarrassed to ask the coach. He found a training manual in the sports section, dog-eared and smelled of someone else's basement, and sat with it under the window while the light turned glacial and gray. There it was, in a chapter on race-day preparation: holding static stretches for a long time, about 60 seconds or more per muscle, right before explosive activity, could briefly reduce strength and power. Many programs therefore warmed up with dynamic movement instead. He read the sentence three times. Sixty seconds or more. He had counted to sixty at every fence post on that cold morning, faithfully, like a good student of his father's method, and he had drained himself at the start line. His father's warm-up wasn't wrong for a Sunday jog. It was wrong for the ten seconds after a gun.

He wanted to blame the book, or the fence, or the rain. Instead he crossed out the warm-up column in his notebook and wrote a new one: leg swings, walking lunges, skips, high knees, all of it moving, none of it held. Rest days kept where they were. He left the stretches in, but moved them to the evening, after the day's work, where they could not take anything from him.

On Wednesday, Danielle was at the fence by the start line early, folded into a long hamstring stretch, and she did not look like someone being lazy. She looked like someone preparing, carefully, to finally take the fourth relay spot at Friday's time trial. Daniel stood beside her with his notebook closed in his hand, and did not open it.

"You're going to feel flat," he said. "Like someone let the air out."

"In the trial?" she said. "I feel flat every trial. That's just trials."

"Come warm up with me," he said. "Moving stuff. Leg swings, skips." He turned the notebook over so she couldn't see that the page was shaking slightly with the wind, or maybe not the wind. "Trust me for one afternoon. If you feel flat anyway, you can go back to the fence."

Danielle unfolded herself from the stretch, slowly, and looked down the straightaway toward the blocks as if the trial were already happening, the finish line already waiting to tell her something.

"Skips first," she said. "Show me."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2018 World Cup in Russia was the first to use video assistant referees, who can review goals, penalties, direct red cards and cases of mistaken identity.
story:
The projector screen went up on the side of the storage shed at ten past four, and by half past, the community field had filled with folding chairs, coolers, and at least forty people facing the white sheet the way they might face a bonfire. Mr. Zhang, who owned the projector and had run the extension cord from the canteen, adjusted the image until the players on the field in Russia looked almost solid against the wrinkled fabric. Michael sat between his father and Kaylee, with Alaa two chairs over, holding a bag of chips he had no intention of sharing.

It was the semifinal, England against Croatia, and England had scored in the fifth minute. Michael's father stood up and knocked his chair backward into a toddler, who did not cry, only stared at him. For most of the match the crowd did its crowd work, groaning at near misses, shouting advice to men five thousand kilometres away, and Michael let himself enjoy the noise the way he enjoyed thunderstorms, as something large that wanted nothing from him.

Croatia equalized in the thirty-ninth minute, and then, in the sixty-eighth, Mandzukic put the ball in off a defender's boot, and everything changed. Mr. Zhang lifted the remote and paused it, then unpaused it, then paused it again, because a man near the canteen was insisting the scorer had been offside. "They'll check it," the man said. "At this World Cup they have the video assistant referees. It's the first time, here in Russia."

"First time at a World Cup," Alaa said, correcting him without looking up from his phone. "And they don't check just anything. Goals, penalties, straight red cards, and if they've booked the wrong player. Mistaken identity, that's the fourth one." He turned the phone around so Kaylee could see the list, as if the list were the argument.

"Then it's football for people who like spreadsheets," Michael's father said. He was still standing. "You cannot commodify a goal into a set of correct angles and sell it back to me as sport. The whole point of the game is that it's watched by human eyes and judged by a man with a whistle and a bad angle and a heartbeat."

Kaylee pulled a leaf off the hedge behind her and shredded it into her cup holder. "You like it when the heartbeat works for you," she said. "Croatia equalized from a set piece your keeper should have claimed, and I didn't hear any speeches about the soul of football then."

Michael had been on his father's side all tournament, more or less by inheritance. He liked the idea that the game was imperfect on purpose, that a wrong call in 1986 was still being argued about at this field tonight because argument was part of what the sport was for. But he had also spent the spring refereeing under-twelves on this same pitch for forty dollars a Saturday, and he remembered a handball in the box he hadn't seen, and a father who had followed him to the parking lot, and the flat affective fact that he had gone home and been sick. He had wanted eyes in the sky then. He was sure of it. He had wanted it more than he had ever wanted anything about the under-twelves.

On the screen, the referee stood with his hand at his ear. The stadium in Russia waited. The field in their own town waited too, and the waiting had a texture Michael had not expected, a shared held breath that felt less like spreadsheet and more like weather. Whatever the video assistant referees were doing in their room, it was producing something here, a roomful of people all suspended in the same second. It occurred to him that the machine had not removed the human part of the game; it had relocated it, gathered it up and concentrated it into these minutes, the way a lens gathers daylight.

"You said it's the first World Cup with it," Michael said to Alaa. "The video people."

"Video assistant referees. Yes. Russia, 2018. Goals, penalties, direct reds, mistaken identity. Nothing else, they don't review a throw-in."

"So a keeper being clattered after the ball's gone, that's nothing. But the same clatter if a penalty's given, that's reviewable." Michael worked through it aloud, watching the referee's ear. It was a narrower thing than he'd assumed. Not a machine that judged everything, but a machine that judged four things and left the rest to the heartbeat, and he could not decide whether that was a compromise or a contradiction, whether the game had been made fairer or merely made to promise a fairness it still couldn't deliver. He suspected both. He suspected he'd still be unsure when he was his father's age, and that his father had been sure at seventeen.

The referee drew a rectangle in the air. Goal given. Croatia led. Michael's father sat down heavily and put his hand on Michael's shoulder, the affective weight of it plain enough, and Kaylee stood and cupped her hands around her mouth. "See," she shouted to no one and everyone, "the spreadsheet loves you back."

On the screen the players walked back to the centre circle, twenty-two small men on a sheet, and Mr. Zhang turned the volume up one bar.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: Historiography is the study of how history has been written, including how historians' interpretations of the same events have changed over time.
story:
Hudson had promised his grandmother he would find the museum's copy of her old schoolbook, the one she swore told the story of the border war "properly, the way it actually was." She had lent him her own battered volume two weeks ago, its margins soft with pencil, and he had carried it in his backpack since, hoping that seeing it under glass would settle something he could not yet name. Now he stood in the long gallery of the regional museum with the book's twin displayed under a pane of glass, open to a page that described the war in three confident paragraphs.

Lennon leaned over his shoulder, chewing the stem of her glasses. "That's it? That's what we took the bus for?"

"Her version has a whole chapter," Hudson said. "This one's shorter."

"So it's the same book."

He compared them, his grandmother's copy open on his palm beside the case. The words matched, sentence for sentence, but the museum's placard beside it said something his grandmother's margin notes never had: that the textbook's account drew on dispatches from a single side, and that later historians had come to read the same events differently. He read the placard twice. The second time, a phrase snagged him, and he copied it into his phone: historiography.

"His what?" Lennon said.

"Historiography," he said. "It's the study of how history has been written. Like, how interpretations of the same events have changed over time."

"So it's history about history."

"I think that's the joke people make about it, yeah."

Lyle arrived late, as he always did, smelling faintly of the parking lot and carrying a soda he was not supposed to have inside. He read the placard upside down first, then right side up, and shrugged. "So the book lied."

"It didn't lie," Hudson said. "It just... didn't have everything. Or asked different questions."

"Same thing."

"It's not the same thing." He heard how stubborn he sounded and lowered his voice. A docent at the far end of the gallery, a small woman with a lanyard, glanced over. Hudson recognized her from somewhere, and then placed her: Ms. Santoso, who had substitute-taught his world history class in the spring. She had spent one memorable period dismantling a turgid essay he had written about the war's causes, telling him his prose was "dressed for a funeral nobody attended." He had not loved her for it at the time.

He waved her over anyway. "Ms. Santoso. Do you have a second?"

She looked at the open grandmother-book in his hand, at the case, at the placard, and her face did something between amusement and recognition. "Whose is that?"

"My grandmother's. She says this textbook is the truth about the war. My textbook at school says something else entirely. I figured one of them was wrong." He turned the old book over in his hands. "But the placard says the dispatches were partial. So the schoolbook wasn't lying. It was just working with what it had. And then people asked new questions."

"Who told you that?"

"Nobody. I mean, the placard kind of did. And it says the word."

"The word does a lot of work," she said. "Some pedagogue probably put it there to frighten visitors, but you seem to have survived."

Lennon laughed. Lyle asked whether the newer textbook could also turn out to be partial, and Hudson felt the question land somewhere behind his ribs, because he had been circling the same one without letting it finish. If interpretations changed over time, then his own textbook was just the newest interpretation, not the last one. His teacher's questions were not his grandmother's questions, and his grandmother's were not the ones historians were asking now, and his own, whatever they were, would look dated to somebody in fifty years.

"I came here to figure out which one was true," he said. "My grandmother wants me to tell her the school is wrong. Or that she is. Somebody gets to be right."

Ms. Santoso did not rescue him from it. She looked at the case and said, "What are you going to tell her?"

He stood there while a school group filed past, their sneakers squeaking, their own docent's voice rising and falling like weather. He thought about how his grandmother had been inured to one story for seventy years, had lived inside it the way you live inside a house you no longer notice, and how tearing a wall out of it would not make the house truer, only colder.
