But leaving it standing felt like a lie by omission. There had to be a way to say both things: that her book was faithful to its sources, and that its sources were not the whole of it. That the truth was larger than either version and kept changing shape as people kept asking.

"Maybe I tell her what the placard says," he said slowly, "and let her decide what to do with it. Not correct her. Just put them side by side, like this." He held the old book up beside the glass so the two identical pages faced each other, the same words in two different frames.

Lennon took a photograph of it before he could lower his hands. "For your grandmother," she said.

"For the essay I'm apparently writing now," Lyle said, and groaned.

Hudson slid the old book back into his backpack, careful with the cracked spine, and copied the rest of the placard into his phone, word for word, questions and all.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own, published in 1929, argues that a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction.
story:
Autumn had claimed the table by the window because its light was honest, neither warm nor cold, and because from there she could watch the automatic doors open for people who knew what they wanted. She had Jane Eyre open to the passage where Jane leaves Thornfield, and beside it a worksheet from Ms. Diallo that read, Apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to one passage. Explain what the lens reveals and what it conceals.

She had chosen the feminist lens first because it seemed easier, and then discovered it was not. Jane walking out onto the moor with nothing, Autumn could see, was a kind of freedom, but it was also a kind of starvation, and the lens did not seem to have a place for both at once. She wrote a sentence and crossed it out. She wrote another and crossed that out too, until the margin of her page looked like a field after a storm.

Tabitha dropped into the chair opposite her with a stack of returns. "You look like the book insulted you."

"It kind of did." Autumn turned the worksheet so Tabitha could see. "Ms. Diallo wants a lens. Like one lens. But if Jane's problem is that she's a woman, that's one thing, and if her problem is that she has no money, that's another, and the passage keeps making them the same problem."

"That's not allowed?"

"It's not that it's not allowed. It's that I can't tell which one the book thinks is doing the work."

Dale arrived with a granola bar he was not supposed to have in the library, and leaned over the worksheet. "Do the Marxist one. Just say everything's about money and you're done. That's what Dev did last semester and he got an A."

"Dev also said Frankenstein was about electricity." Tabitha took the granola bar and put it in her bag, which was her way of confiscating it.

Autumn said nothing, because a thought had started in her and she did not want to break it. The doors hissed open and closed. Somewhere near the front desk, Ms. Diallo was shelving returns, and Autumn watched her move a cart of books with the unhurried competence of someone who had answered every question the building could produce. Autumn raised her hand anyway, which made Tabitha laugh, and Ms. Diallo came over.

"Are you allowed to tell me if I'm allowed to use two lenses?" Autumn asked.

"I'm allowed to tell you the assignment says one." Ms. Diallo pulled out the chair beside her and sat, which surprised Autumn, who had expected a verdict from a standing position, like a judge's. "But you didn't ask me that. You asked me if you were allowed."

"It feels like cheating. Like I can't pick, so I'm picking both."

"Or like the passage can't pick," Ms. Diallo said. "I'd start with the reading list question. Dale asked it in class on Monday."

Dale looked up, startled to be included. "I asked why like half the books were by guys. Mostly guys. Way mostly."

"And what did we find?"

"That the women were writing too. Some of them. Just less got kept."

Ms. Diallo stood, and instead of a lecture she left them with a direction: the criticism shelves, one specific shelf, third from the bottom. "Look for a slim book. Orange spine. It's short, which for once is in your favor."

The shelf was in the quiet section, where the carpet was older and the light came down in strips. Autumn crouched and found the orange spine almost immediately, as though it had been waiting to be asked. She read the first pages standing up, one hand on the shelf for balance, and the argument arrived in her not as information but as recognition. A woman who wanted to write fiction, the book said, published in 1929, needed money and a room of her own. Autumn read the sentence twice. It was not that women had nothing to say, or said it badly. It was that they had been given no money and no room, and from nothing, nothing follows.

She carried it back to the table with the care of someone transporting something breakable. "Okay," she said, sitting down. "Dale. Your question. This is the answer, or part of it. Virginia Woolf, 1929, A Room of One's Own. She says a woman has to have money and a room of her own if she's going to write fiction. That's the whole condition. Money and a room."

"So the reading list is mostly men because..." Dale stopped, and Autumn watched him get there himself. "Because of rooms."

"And money," Tabitha said. "You can't leave out the money, that's the whole thing, they go together."

Autumn opened Jane Eyre again, and now the passage did something it had not done before. Jane on the moor was not merely a woman refusing a man, and not merely a paivist refusing a master; she was a person whom the world had given no money and no room, walking out of the one borrowed room she had, which was exactly the thing Woolf said a woman could not write without. The lens had seemed like a machine for simplifying, but held at the right angle it transfigured the page instead, and the two lenses she could not choose between folded into each other like hands. At the same time something was lost. Jane stopped being purely a heroine to her, became also a case, a datum in an argument about rooms, and Autumn felt the small grief of that, the way understanding always charges a fee.

She began to write, slowly, leaving one sentence unfinished because she did not yet know its end. She wrote that the Marxist lens and the feminist lens were not rivals here but auxiliary to each other, each supplying what the other lacked, and then she stopped at the word acquittal, which she had wanted to use about Rochester, and could not make honest, because Rochester was not acquitted, and neither was the world that built him, and neither, she suspected, was her own essay going to be. She left a blank where the conclusion would go.

Tabitha read over her shoulder. "You're not going to finish it tonight."

"No," Autumn said. She closed the Woolf and kept her thumb in Jane Eyre. "But I know where the room is now."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: German capitalizes every noun, not only names, which helps a reader of a German article spot the nouns in a sentence at a glance.
story:
The article was only four paragraphs long, and Katherine had been staring at it for the better part of an hour. It came from a German newspaper, a short piece about a city council debating whether to sell a parcel of land, and Mr. De Vries had assigned it to her with the mild confidence of a man who believed she could do more than she believed she could. On Thursday she would have to stand up in the language lab and summarise it aloud, in German, in front of the whole class.

The problem was not the dictionary. She had a good dictionary, and the words were ordinary ones: city, money, year, decision. The problem was the sentences themselves, which seemed to go on for whole lines before revealing where their weight lay. She could not tell what belonged to whom. Halfway through the second paragraph she noticed, for the first time, how many words began with capital letters. Not just the ones at the start of sentences. Words in the middle, ordinary words, standing up proudly in the middle of the line like they owned the place.

She counted them. In the first sentence alone there were six.

Maxym slid into the chair across from her with his own assignment, a French one, and set up his flashcards in a slow deliberate fan. "Still on the land thing?" he said. "Brenna finished hers last night. She said it took her forty minutes."

"It's not a race," Katherine said, though she felt the truth of it anyway, the small bruise of being behind. She turned the paper toward him. "Look at this. Why are all these words capitalized? Rats? City? Is that a name I don't know?"

Maxym squinted at it the way he squinted at everything, as though the world were slightly out of focus. "No idea. Maybe German does that. Maybe they capitalize words that matter."

"But the city is the subject and the money isn't capitalized," she said, and stopped, because that wasn't right either, and she knew it wasn't right, and she was tired of guessing.

The library around them had gone quiet in the way it did after four o'clock, the interminable hiss of the radiators the only sound. Behind the desk Mr. De Vries was cataloguing a box of donated books, and Katherine watched him work for a moment before she got up and carried the article over to him.

"I have a question, but I don't want the answer given to me," she said.

"That's a very specific request," Mr. De Vries said, and did not look up from the box.

"The capital letters. In the middle of sentences. There are too many of them and I can't find the pattern."

He set down a book, considered her, and said only this: "German capitalizes every noun, not only names."

She stood there while it rearranged itself in her head. Not the important words. The nouns, all of them, always. She went back to her table without thanking him, which she would feel slightly guilty about later, and sat down and read the first sentence again with her finger under each capitalized word. Stadt. Rat. Land. Verkauf. It was like someone had gone through the sentence beforehand and marked every noun for her. She could see the skeleton of it at a glance, the bones standing out from the flesh of the verbs and prepositions, and once she saw the bones the rest began to hang on them.

"Find it?" Maxym said.

"Every noun," she said. "All of them, even the boring ones. It's like the language is doing half my work for me." She was already parsing the second paragraph, and the third, and where before there had been a wall of grey type there was now a kind of architecture, load-bearing words in plain sight.

She started drafting the summary on the back of a receipt from the vending machine. The council wanted to sell the land, but a citizens' group had collected signatures against it, and the vote would come in the autumn. She wrote it out in clumsy German, read it aloud under her breath, and heard how wooden it sounded, every word fetched separately and set down like furniture being moved by one person.

She thought, briefly, of quitting German the way she had quit piano at eleven, an afternoon when she had closed the lid on the keys and told her mother she was bored, and had known even then that boredom was not the true reason, that the true reason was that the pieces had begun to ask more of her than she wanted to give. Her mother had said only, all right, and paid out the remaining month of lessons like a small annuity of disappointment, a fixed sum arriving every week until the term ran out. Katherine had felt emancipated by the decision for about a month, and then had simply stopped thinking about it. She did not want this to be like that. But she also knew that wanting was not a plan.

Brenna arrived at five, dropping her bag on the table with the ease of someone finished. "Want me to listen to it?" she offered.

"It's terrible," Katherine said.

"Read it anyway."

Katherine read it anyway, slowly, mispronouncing Herbst and going back for it, and when she finished Brenna nodded the way friends nod at things that are not yet good. "The middle part," Brenna said. "You said the group collected signatures. Is that the group against the sale or the citizens' group generally? It's the same word."

Katherine looked at the article again. The same word, capitalized like every other noun, standing there in the middle of the sentence, and it could be either, and the dictionary would not tell her which, and on Thursday she would have to choose.

"I don't know yet," she said, and picked up her pen.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Near the edges of real plates the field lines bulge outward and the field weakens, an effect called fringing, so E = V/d holds best near the centre.
story:
Brooke set the two aluminum plates on the upturned milk crate in her backyard, twelve centimeters apart, propped with rulers because the stands she'd tried to requisition from the physics room had gone to the robotics team first. Usman sat cross-legged in the grass beside her, holding the voltmeter like it might bite. The evening smelled of cut grass and the neighbor's charcoal, and above them the sky was doing that slow orange-to-violet thing she never got tired of watching, even with a lab due Monday.

"Twelve centimeters," she said. "Nine volts across the plates. So E equals V over d. Nine divided by zero point one two." She wrote it in the margin of her notebook: seventy-five volts per meter. It had seemed almost arrogant, the first time Ms. Nakamura had shown them, how three symbols could claim to know what an invisible field was doing everywhere between two plates.

The flashback came without warning, the way good memories did. She was eight, in this same backyard, holding two magnets under a sheet of paper while her father sprinkled iron filings and told her to watch. The filings had lined up into curves, bending toward each other at the ends, like they were leaning in to whisper. She had asked him why they curved instead of going straight, and he had said, honestly, that he didn't know, and that not knowing was her job now. She had liked the way that sounded, like being handed something.

"Ready?" Usman attached the charge sensor to the wand, a discarded kabob skewer taped to a chopstick, its tip positioned between the plates. Brooke had spent two evenings on the wand alone. At the center, the sensor read close to what the formula promised, and they both exhaled. Then, because Brooke was the kind of person who couldn't leave a good number alone, she slid the wand toward the right edge, centimeter by centimeter, watching the reading on her phone.

It fell. Not dramatically, but unmistakably, from seventy-five toward sixty-something as the tip approached the edge of the plate, then dropped faster just past it. "That's wrong," Usman said. "Or the formula's wrong. Or your wand's garbage." He said it cheerfully, the way he said everything, but Brooke felt the specific sting of a prediction failing. She moved the wand back toward the center and watched the number climb again, steady and obedient, like a dog returning to its yard.

"Or the formula is only true somewhere," she said slowly. It was a thought she'd been circling all week, ever since Ms. Nakamura had written E equals V over d on the board and then, in a move Brooke still wondered about, drawn the plates as finite rectangles instead of infinite lines. What had she been hinting at? Was the equation a description or an idealization, the way a map of homeostasis in biology class had turned out to be a simplification of a body that was actually improvising every second? Brooke sat back on her heels and looked at the gap between the plates, trying to see the field the way the iron filings had once shown her magnets, wondering whether it bulged.

That night she wrote to Ms. Nakamura, because office hours were over and because some questions felt too soft for the classroom. "I measured between the plates and got the right value near the middle, but it drops near the edge. Usman thinks our equipment is bad. I think the field does something different out there, maybe curves like the iron filings did with my dad's magnets. Is the formula lying to us, or are we lying to ourselves when we use it everywhere?" She read it twice, deleted "lying" and put it back, and sent it before she could get canny about it.

The reply came the next morning, short enough to fit on her phone without scrolling. "Your equipment sounds fine. Look up what happens to the field lines at the edges of real plates. Then tell me where your formula holds best. I'm curious what you'll decide counts as the middle." No answer, really. A door held open.

In the backyard again, after school, she and Usman searched on his phone. The pictures came up immediately, field lines drawn between two plates, straight and parallel in the center, and then, near the edges, curving outward, spreading like hair pushed back from a face. "Fringing," Usman read aloud. "It's called fringing." Brooke stared at the diagrams, feeling the small click of two things meeting: her father's iron filings bending, her sensor's numbers falling, the pictures on the screen. Near the edges of real plates the field lines bulged outward and the field weakened, so E equals V over d held best near the centre, and her measurements had not been wrong at all. They had been telling her where the equation lived and where it didn't.

"So the whole formula is just a middle-of-the-plate thing," Usman said, poking the wand toward the center again, as if to make the number prove it once more. The reading climbed back to seventy-five and sat there, steady, certain of itself, while a June bug droned past the plate's edge and vanished into the grass.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In US college admissions, a college's yield is the percentage of students it admits who then accept the offer and enroll.
story:
The portal had been showing the same grey bar for eleven days, and Alexandre had begun to refresh it the way his grandfather used to jiggle a radio dial, as though the answer were already in the machine and only needed coaxing out. He sat at the desk in the corner of the kitchen with his application number written on a Post-it beside the keyboard, though he had memorized it by the second day. Early Decision, binding, to a college three states away. He had clicked the agreement box in October without letting himself read the paragraph twice, because reading it twice would have meant thinking about what binding meant, and thinking about it in October might have meant not clicking at all.

The tour in August was where the trouble started, though he hadn't known it then. He and Kohen had driven up with Alexandre's mother, who pretended the campus bookstore was not a trap and bought a sweatshirt anyway. The guide, a senior with a voice like a park announcer, stood beneath an oak and said the school's yield was the highest in its history. Kohen, who never let a word go by unexamined, raised his hand. "What's yield?" Alexandre looked it up on his phone while the guide finished the sentence, and then leaned over and said it quietly, so the group wouldn't stop moving. "It's the percentage of students a college admits who then accept the offer and enroll."

Kohen had nodded and moved on, but Alexandre had stood there for a second longer, feeling something rearrange itself. The college was not only choosing them. They were choosing it, and the choosing was counted, weighed, boasted about under an oak tree by a senior in a polo. When the Early Decision agreement arrived in his inbox two months later, he understood, in a way he hadn't in August, that clicking yes made him part of that number before he even knew the number wanted him.

His mother passed behind him with a dish towel and set a mug of tea at his elbow without comment, the way she had done every evening since December, as though the mug were a small argument against checking. He drank it anyway. She had wanted him closer to home; she had said so exactly once, in the car after the tour, and then never again, which was its own kind of stoic. He had learned to read her through what she didn't repeat. The tea was chamomile. He had never told her he liked chamomile.

At nine his phone buzzed. Eliot, who had applied regular decision everywhere and treated the whole season with the detachment of someone watching weather happen to other people. "any movement?" "no." "my cousin says they release ED mid-December." "i know." He typed that and then deleted it and wrote instead, "how's your grandma?" because Eliot's grandmother had been in the hospital since Thanksgiving, and Eliot had gone quiet in the group chat the way people do when the important thing isn't the thing everyone else is talking about. "better. they basically resuscitated her in the hallway. she's mad about the bill." Alexandre laughed, alone, at the kitchen desk, and it loosened something in his chest.

Ms. Tang from next door knocked at half past nine with a container of dumplings, because she had seen the lights on and had decided, as she always had, that lights on at this hour meant a boy needed feeding. She asked about the letter without asking, the way she asked about everything. "Still the computer," he said, and she made a sound that meant she thought the whole system was a nonsense, which it probably was, and left the dumplings on the counter with instructions he already knew.

He went back to the desk, but he didn't refresh right away. He opened instead the folder where he kept the screenshots, the tour photos, the paragraph he had finally allowed himself to reread in November, the one about withdrawing all other applications if admitted. He had applied nowhere else. That was the part Kohen had called insane, in a friendly way, at lunch, and Alexandre had defended it then with a certainty that now felt borrowed. He could admit, at least to the dark kitchen window, that he didn't know whether he had chosen the college or chosen to be chosen, and that the yield, whatever it turned out to be, couldn't answer that for him. Both things could be true. He let them sit side by side, unreconciled, like the two mugs on the desk.

At ten past ten the grey bar changed. Not to the answer; only to a message saying decisions would be released tomorrow at five. He sat with that for a moment, then picked up his phone and typed to Eliot, "tomorrow 5pm," and to Kohen, separately, "come over after?" He drank the cold chamomile and carried the dumplings to Ms. Tang's door, still warm through the plastic, and knocked twice.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Silvio Berlusconi kept control of Mediaset, owner of three of Italy's main national TV channels, while serving as the country's prime minister.
story:
The notification lit up at 11:47, while Makayla was still rinsing her mother's coffee mug and stacking the dishwasher without being asked, because her mother had taken the early shift again. The group chat, nineteen messages deep, was titled "Ramos op-ed WAR ROOM," and Dave had kicked it off with a screenshot of a local headline: Millbrook Ledger Acquired by Harrow Resources. Nobody outside the chat had said a word about it yet, but Karlee had typed, "ok but does it even matter who owns a paper," and Dave had replied with a single angry period, which in his language meant he was already writing a paragraph.

Makayla dried her hands and typed, "meet at Perk tomorrow, 4. bring the assignment sheet." Ms. Ramos had given them two weeks to write an op-ed on any issue involving "how we know what we know," which was the kind of assignment that sounded easy until you actually tried to find something you could prove. Makayla wanted the Harrow story. The mine wanted to expand into the watershed, her mother had opinions about the watershed, and now the company that wanted the expansion owned the only paper in town that would print her opinions. That was an issue involving how we know what we know, she figured, if she could find a way to say it that didn't sound like a conspiracy theory typed in all caps.

At Perk the next afternoon, Karlee had spread her marine biology flashcards across half the table before anyone else arrived, pelagic zone, pelagic birds, pelagic trawlers, and she moved them into a stack the moment Makayla came through the door, smoothing the space clear like a small apology. "I have the quiz Friday," Karlee said. "Sit. You look like you read the whole internet last night."

"I read some of it," Makayla said. "Dave, you quiet down for a second, I want to try something on you both." Dave had a whole argument prepared, she could tell, about money and power and the spinelessness of local media, and he had a way of delivering paragraphs like a door swinging open that knocked everyone else out of the conversation. She held up her phone. "Say you're an average person in Italy, like twenty years ago. Who do you trust to tell you what your prime minister is doing?"

"The news," Karlee said, frowning at a flashcard she'd rescued from under the napkin dispenser.

"Right. Now say the prime minister owns most of what you're watching." Dave opened his mouth and she talked faster, which was a thing she had inured herself to doing around him over four years of group projects, apologizing to him later, always, but not stopping. "Silvio Berlusconi kept control of Mediaset while he was serving as the country's prime minister," she said. "Mediaset owned three of Italy's main national TV channels. Same guy. Three channels, and he's the one they're covering."

Karlee set down the flashcard. "That's allowed?"

"It happened," Makayla said. "I checked it twice, because it sounded like something Dave would make up."

"It does not sound like something I would make up," Dave said. "It sounds like something I would be right about."

"That's what I mean though," Karlee said slowly, turning her cup so the handle faced the window, a habit of hers when she was actually thinking. "If it can be that obvious there, then it's probably happening here in ways that aren't obvious. Which is worse." She looked at her flashcards, then back up. "But I still don't know what a person is supposed to do with that. Stop watching TV? Everything's owned by somebody."

Makayla had her notebook open by then, and she wrote can't opt out and underneath it, so what instead. She admitted to them, honestly, that she didn't know either. Her first draft the night before had ended with a sentence about readers deserving the whole truth, and she had deleted it because it had the verisimilitude of a greeting card, it resembled conviction without containing any. What she actually believed was smaller and harder: that ownership was worth knowing about, the way you'd want to know a courtroom judge was the defendant's uncle. Knowing didn't fix anything by itself. Not knowing fixed even less.

"Here's what I want to run with," she said. "Not that Harrow is evil. I can't prove that, and honestly the mine might bring jobs, my mom's not even sure she's against it. Just: when you read the Ledger now, you should know who signs the paychecks, the same way Italians knew whose channels they were watching. Then people can decide for themselves whether the coverage smells off." She pushed the notebook across so they could see her outline. "Dave tears it apart. Karlee, tell me if it sounds naive."

Dave read it twice, which was more patience than he usually spent on anything. "The Berlusconi part is strong," he said. "Keep the number exactly right, three channels, because if you get it wrong they'll use it to dismiss everything else." Karlee tapped the last line of the outline and said the ending needed a person in it, not a principle, and offered to proofread Friday after her quiz, and she re-stacked her flashcards and slid them into her bag to give them the table, and Makayla noticed that and said thank you in a way that meant more than the words.

She didn't send the op-ed that night. She sat at the kitchen table after her mother came home smelling of the hospital cafeteria, and she read her last paragraph aloud once to hear whether it held. "Ownership doesn't tell you a story is false," she'd written. "It tells you who was in the room when the story got shaped." Her mother said it sounded true, and then asked if Makayla wanted the rest of her soup, and pushed the bowl across before she answered.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: The dependency ratio compares people aged under 15 and 65 and over with people aged 15 to 64, estimating how many dependents each working-age person supports.
story:
The trail rose through pine shade for the first kilometre, then broke open onto a granite shoulder where the whole valley lay below them, quilted with farm fields and one pale thread of highway. Mr. Rosen called a rest stop, unshouldered his daypack, and began handing out laminated sheets, one per pair. Justine unfolded hers on a flat rock. Two bar graphs stood back to back like a butterfly, one heavy at the bottom with a wide base of children, the other bulging at the top like an onion on a stick.

"Kenya and Japan," said Ayla, reading the small print. "Guess which is which."

"Naya gets the onion," Justine said, because Naya had wedged herself between them on the bus and now claimed a share of the rock, and because sharing meant she had to explain things out loud, which was the whole reason Mr. Rosen called these field days "walking seminars," a phrase Naya found so ascetic it made her hungry. She was already unwrapping a granola bar.

Mr. Rosen drifted past with his hands clasped behind him. "Question for the group," he said. "You're the minister of finance. Your pyramid looks like the onion. Twenty years from now, do you build schools or nursing homes?"

Naya, instantly political, asked whether the ministry was secular or sectarian, because in her grandmother's country, she said, you could not build so much as a bus shelter without somebody claiming the land for a temple. Ayla said that was not the point. Justine said it sort of was the point, actually, and then felt the familiar heat in her ears, because she was the one who never spoke first and now she had, and both of them were looking at her.

So she committed. "Look at the bars," she said, tapping the Japanese pyramid. "It's like a class photo where everyone's the same age. All those people in the middle, the working ones, they're the shoulders holding everybody else up. The little kids and the old people, they're being carried."

"You just made that up," said Ayla, but she was squinting at the sheet.

"There's a thing for it," Justine said. "We did it Tuesday. It's called the dependency ratio. It compares people aged under 15 and 65 and over with people aged 15 to 64, and it estimates how many dependents each working-age person supports." She had written it on her hand before the quiz, which Naya had told her was the most delinquent thing she'd ever done, this from a girl who once climbed out a first-floor window to avoid a piano recital.

I hadn't thought about it again until Dad called that night, which is where I have to pick the story up myself, because I was the only one who knew what the call was about. I was lying on my bed with the pyramid still in my bag, still creased from being unfolded on granite, when his voice came through the speaker flat and tired, the way it got in the months after the mill announced the shifts were changing. He'd heard something on the radio about the pension levy going up again and he wanted to know, since I was suddenly the college-bound one, whether the radio was lying to him.

"Sort of lying and sort of not," I said, and I could hear him settle in, the creak of the kitchen chair, the sound of him deciding to be patient.

"Explain like I'm your father," he said, "because I am."

So I told him about the class photo. About carrying people. About how the radio man probably lived in a country shaped like our onion, where every year the middle of the pyramid thins a little and the top widens, and the ratio shifts, and the levy climbs to keep pace, and none of it is anybody's fault, exactly, it is just arithmetic doing what arithmetic does. I said the words again, the whole fact, slow this time, and when I finished there was a silence long enough that I checked whether the call had dropped.

"Every working person," he said finally, "carrying more each year."

"Each working-age person," I said, because he'd earned the precision, and he laughed, a real one, and said, "Hun, half the men I know are working-age and incapacitated by the end of a shift, but I take your meaning."

Here's what I didn't tell him, because I hadn't worked it out yet and I still haven't. The radio man had talked about the levy as if it were a verdict on people's character, as if the old had somehow voted themselves expensive. And my ratio, my clean little fraction, treats every person under fifteen and over sixty-four as a weight and every person between as a bearer, which is true enough for a quiz and not obviously true at all for a life. Dad is fifty-one and carrying my grandmother and, technically, me. My grandmother raised four kids and paid into the levy for forty years; calling her a dependent seemed like a strange way to thank her. Kenya's pyramid said build schools, Japan's said build nursing homes, and both answers felt, sitting on that rock with Ayla's knee against mine, like the beginning of a question rather than the end of one.

The next morning Ayla texted me a photo she'd taken on the trail, the two of us bent over the sheet, Naya's granola bar mid-air in the corner of the frame. "Mr. Rosen says bring the pyramids Monday," the caption read. "He wants to know what a country owes its old and what it owes its young, and he says we have forty minutes and no answers."

I texted back, "Tell him forty minutes won't be enough," and started pulling my boots on.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Lunar New Year, many Chinese families give money in red envelopes to children and unmarried younger relatives, because red is associated with good fortune and warding off evil.
story:
The cultural center smelled of fried sesame balls and incense, and Xavier stood near the folding tables with his hands in his pockets, trying to look like a boy who belonged at exactly this level of festivity. His grandmother had shoved him through the doors an hour ago with the instruction to "go be young somewhere," which he suspected was a hint about the red envelopes being distributed at the far table. He was sixteen. He was, by most reckonings, still a child. But he was also tall enough that the cashier at the movie theater had stopped asking if he wanted the kids' popcorn combo, and the question of the envelopes had begun to feel genuinely urgent.

"Are you lurking," said Melyna, appearing beside him with a paper plate of dumplings, "or hiding?"

"Reconnaissance," Xavier said. At the far table, an aunt he only saw once a year was pressing small red envelopes into the hands of children and, he noticed, of his cousin Wei, who was nineteen, unmarried, and technically his elder by three years. Wei took his envelope with the unbothered confidence of a man collecting rent.

"Because Deklan's over there asking people about the decorations," Melyna said, "and one grandmother called him a scholar and gave him an envelope for being polite. He didn't even know what it was. He thought it was a birthday card."

Xavier watched Deklan across the room, bowing slightly, holding the red rectangle up to the light like a rare stamp. Something in Xavier turned sour and interesting at once. Deklan had no lineage here, no grandmother in the corner saving him a seat, no memory of licking sesame paste off his fingers at this exact table in earlier, shorter years. And Deklan had an envelope, and Xavier did not.

He went to find Mr. Szabó, who ran the center and could usually be counted on for a straight answer between rounds of refilling the tea urn. Mr. Szabó was refilling the tea urn.

"The envelopes," Xavier said. "Is sixteen too old?"

Mr. Szabó screwed the lid back onto the urn. "Too old for what? I hand them out; I don't write the rules."

"You're equivocating."

"I'm being tactful." But he nodded toward the table. "Watch who gets them. It's children, and it's the unmarried younger relatives. Mostly it's about being the young side of the family. Your cousin Wei, he still counts. You, you're still squarely a child by any standard I'd defend."

"Sixteen is not squarely a child."

"Then don't tell anyone I said so."

Xavier drifted back toward Melyna, who was now engaged in what could only be described as a dumpling evaluation, weighing two identical dumplings in each palm. "So?" she said.

"So I qualify. But Wei also qualifies, and he's nineteen, which means the cutoff is not age, it's something else. Status, maybe. Unmarried and junior in the family. Which means I could technically keep collecting until I'm old enough to have a mortgage."

"Romantic," Melyna said. "You've turned a New Year gift into a subscription service."

"It's not about the money," Xavier said, and heard, even as he said it, how the sentence was a small lie. The money was five dollars, sometimes ten. It was about the envelope itself, the red of it, bright as a firecracker, and the idea that red carried good fortune and kept evil away, which his grandmother had said exactly once and never repeated, as if it were too obvious to mention. He liked belonging to a thing that treated a color as a working tool.

His grandmother waved him over then, and he went, and she pressed an envelope into his hand with a grip that suggested he should not equivocate about accepting it. "Even big ones need luck," she said. "Especially big ones."

"I'm not big," he said, pocketing it. "I'm sixteen."

"Enormous," she said. "A giant. Sit, eat."

He sat, and Deklan folded into the chair beside him holding his own envelope, and a small argument broke out between Deklan and Melyna about whether the sesame balls were better than the dumplings, an argument that became briefly vitriolic when Deklan claimed sesame balls were "objectively superior" and Melyna called him a dictator of dessert. Xavier laughed into his tea. He still wasn't sure where the line fell, whether at nineteen or at marriage or at some age his aunts decided by committee, and he found he liked not knowing, liked having a rule that bent to fit the family rather than the other way around.

Later, at the door, his grandmother adjusted his collar and said, "Next year too."

"Next year what?"

She patted his pocket, where the envelope sat, and turned back toward the folding tables.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: Molar mass in grams per mole has the same number as a particle's average mass in atomic mass units; one carbon atom averages about 12.01 units, and one mole of carbon about 12.01 grams.
story:
The kettle had been on for ten minutes before Leah remembered it, which was the kind of thing that happened at her grandmother's house, where time moved like honey and the chemistry textbook on the kitchen table looked like it had landed from another planet. She was there because the apartment was being repainted and her mother had said go, take your work, your grandmother would love the company. The exam was Monday. Stoichiometry, Chapter 9, the section she had read four times without it opening for her the way other sections had.

"Six point two grams of glucose," she said to the empty kitchen, "reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water, and I am supposed to find the moles of carbon dioxide." The kettle whistled. She got up, poured the water over the tea bag her grandmother had set out that morning before her walk, and sat back down in front of the problem as though staring could transmute the numbers into an answer. It could not. She had the balanced equation, she had the mass, and between them sat something she kept almost grasping and then losing, like a word on the tip of the tongue.

What she kept circling was the periodic table, a paper copy folded out of the back of the textbook, soft at the creases. Under carbon it said 12.01, and in her notes from Mr. Pritchard's class she had written "molar mass: 12.01 g/mol." The same number. She had assumed that was a coincidence of notation, some shorthand teachers used, and had copied it without question the way she copied a lot of things. But now, alone, with nobody to perform understanding for, she looked at it again. One carbon atom, the table said, had an average mass of about 12.01 units, atomic mass units, the little mass of one little atom. And one mole of carbon, a whole enormous pile of it, 6.02 times 10 to the 23 atoms, weighed about 12.01 grams. The same number on both sides, like a bridge she hadn't known she was standing on.

Her phone buzzed on the table. Sylvie, from the study group she had skipped: "did you figure out the sugar problem or are you still being facetious about dropping out to become a shepherd." Leah typed back "still considering the sheep," then, before she could stop herself, "wait. Say carbon's number off your table." Sylvie replied "12.01, why." Leah wrote: "for one atom AND for a mole. grams per mole. same number." There was a long pause, the three dots appearing and vanishing, and then Sylvie sent "?????" followed by "no. wait. NO." and then a string of exclamation marks that made Leah laugh out loud in the quiet kitchen.

She pulled the sugar canister across the table. Glucose was C6H12O6, that much she knew cold. Carbon, 12.01 per atom, so 12.01 grams per mole, times six atoms. Hydrogen, 1.008. Oxygen, 16.00. She added it up twice, got 180.16 both times, and sat with that number a moment before going on. Six point two grams of glucose divided by 180.16 grams per mole gave her the moles of glucose, and the balanced equation said six moles of carbon dioxide for every one of glucose, so she multiplied, and there it was: 0.207 moles. She checked it against the answer in the back of the book, holding her thumb over the page like a card sharp, and it matched. Something in her chest loosened, a knot she hadn't fully registered tying itself.

"It smells like victory in here," her grandmother said from the doorway, still in her coat, a bag of clementines in one hand. "Or like burnt tea."

"Both, probably," Leah said, and realized the tea had gone cold and dark. She moved it aside and turned the notebook around. "Look. I figured something out. That number there, twelve point oh one. It's the mass of one carbon atom, in these tiny units. And it's also the grams in a whole mole of carbon, which is this gigantic number of atoms, like a beach made of sand and then some. Same number." Her grandmother pulled out the other chair and sat, peeling a clementine with slow, exact thumbs.

"A mole," her grandmother said, tasting the word. "Like the thing in the garden?"

"That's what it's called," Leah said. "A mole. There's a whole mole of chemistry jokes about it, none of them good." Her grandmother said that in her day a mole was something you trapped and that was the end of it, and Leah laughed and gave her a section of the clementine, and for a while they just ate it, the sections small and bright, the kitchen going gold at the edges of the afternoon. Leah kept her hand on the notebook. She understood the bridge now, the way the number on the table worked for one atom and for the pile, an isthmus between a world too small to see and a world you could weigh on a kitchen scale, though if you asked her why the same number worked on both sides she would have to say she didn't know yet, not really, and she was tired of pretending otherwise.

The phone buzzed again. Sylvie: "kristopher says he got 0.2 for the sugar one, is that the same as yours??" Leah looked at her 0.207, at Kristopher's 0.2 rounded off, and typed, "close. tell him to keep his decimals," then set the phone face down and slid the sugar canister back toward the counter. "Grandma," she said, "do we have any more problems like this, or do I have to invent them?" and her grandmother, who did not know a mole from a molar but knew a granddaughter who wanted one, pointed at the pantry and said, "There's a whole bag of sugar in there. Knock yourself out."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In The Two Fridas, both women's hearts are exposed, and a single blood vessel connects them, winding through their hands and hearts.
story:
Gavin spread the printout of The Two Fridas across the kitchen table and pinned its corners with the salt shaker, a mug, and a fistful of grapes nobody was eating. The assignment sheet sat beside it, and beside that, his sketchbook, open to a page where he had copied the two women in hasty pencil, badly. Brayden, who had come over supposedly to study for chemistry, leaned across the grapes.

"You drew them like they're waiting for a bus," Brayden said.

"They are waiting for a bus. The bus is called a formal analysis, and it never comes." Gavin tapped the assignment sheet. "Colour, composition, symbolism. Three paragraphs by Friday. Mr. Kowalski says if I write 'it looks sad' one more time he will frame it as a warning to other students."

Charlotte arrived twenty minutes late with her own tablet and a bag of licorice, which she doled out like a doctor deciding who deserved it. She looked at the printout for a long moment, then at Gavin's sketch. "Okay, first, your Fridas have hands like oven mitts. Second, you skipped the best part." She took his pencil and drew a thin line on the sketch, starting at the chest of the Frida in white, looping down through her fingers, across the gap between the two women, and up into the hands and chest of the Frida in blue.

Gavin leaned in. "Wait. That's actually in the painting?"

"Both hearts are exposed. Look. You can see them, right there, both of them. And there's a single blood vessel connecting them. It goes through their hands and their hearts, the whole winding route." She traced it on the printout with her finger, and Gavin followed it himself, pencil hovering, feeling slightly betrayed that he had stared at the thing for two evenings and missed the one red thread that tied everything together.

"So that's the composition," he said slowly, and began sketching it in, his oven-mitt hands suddenly mattering less. "It's not two figures side by side. It's one line. The European one in white, the Mexican one in blue, and the line holds them together whether they like it or not." He thought about the stormy sky behind them, the little portrait the blue Frida holds, the white Frida's scissors and the blood on her dress. "The white one's bleeding where she's cut. The blue one's holding her own heart like it's a locket. Colour does the split, white against blue, but the red is what connects them."

Brayden, who had been pretending to study titration curves this entire time, looked up. "See, this is why I like chemistry. Everything's a titration. You add one thing to another and at some exact point it changes color, and that point means something. You art people just argue."

"Art people," said Gavin, "have an oligarchy of gatekeepers who decided a comma splice is a moral failing, and Mr. Kowalski is their king." He was writing now, fast, his pen scratching through a sentence about how the exposed hearts made the figures vulnerable in a way the stiff, formal pose contradicted. Formal clothes, exposed organs, storm sky. He liked that. He wrote another sentence and crossed out half of it.

"Here's my problem though," he said, stopping. Both of them looked at him, which was rare enough that he paused to enjoy it. "The symbolism part. I can say the two women are two sides of one person, or two countries, or the self before and after something, and Mr. Kowalski wants a considered position. But I can't decide which reading the painting itself supports, or if it supports all of them, and if I pick wrong I'm just decorating a guess." Charlotte offered him the last piece of licorice, which he took as tribute. "I'll write what I think and then say what I can't settle. He can dock me for honesty."

"That's tragically noble," Brayden said. "Also you wrote 'saturnine sky' three times on that page. Once is mysterious. Three is a cry for help."

Gavin crossed out two of them. Charlotte read his opening paragraph out loud in the voice of a documentary narrator, doing the exposed hearts with air quotes, until he threatened to revoke her grape privileges. He kept the red line in his sketch, traced it once more with the pencil, from heart to hands to heart, and left his pencil resting on the exact spot where the vessel crossed between them.

"Now," he said, pulling the chemistry notes toward himself, "titrate me a strong acid before I write 'resplendent' by accident."

"You already did," Charlotte said, turning the page around to show him.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, Muslims who can afford it give a set charity called zakat al-fitr for each family member, so that poor families can also celebrate Eid.
story:
The night before Eid, Laurie sat at the kitchen table while her mother counted out small envelopes, one for each member of the family, and asked Laurie to finish the arithmetic. Her grandmother was convalescing after a fall, so the task had drifted downward, to Laurie, the way household tasks did when someone's hands were suddenly unavailable. At the table she worked it out: before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, Muslims who could afford it gave a set charity for each family member, so that poor families could also celebrate Eid. Her mother had called it zakat al-fitr while spooning sugar into her tea, as if naming it were the whole instruction, and Laurie had written the amounts on each envelope in her looping handwriting. Seven envelopes. Her mother had paused over the eighth, a cousin recently arrived from Lahore with almost nothing, and put it in the pile anyway.

By morning the envelopes had become a memory of paper, and the street outside the mosque had become a festival. Laurie walked it with Antonin, who had converted in February and was, in his own words, still a neophyte at all of this, pointing at tables of baklava and kunafa like a tourist collecting proof of a country he had only read about. He asked her why there were baskets of rice and dates stacked by the mosque doors, and she told him, keeping her voice easy, the way you explain something you learned only twelve hours ago and want to sound certain about. A set charity, before the prayer, for each family member, so that poor families could celebrate Eid too. He nodded and bought them both coffee from a cart, and Laurie drank hers and thought about the eighth envelope, which she had sealed without asking whether the cousin knew she had been counted.

Logan found them near the henna tables, pugnacious as ever about the parking situation, having circled the festival four times in his father's car. He was not Muslim and had come, he claimed, strictly for the food, though Laurie had noticed he also stood quietly through the call to prayer, hands in his pockets, watching the men and women arrange themselves in rows. She remembered a night in tenth grade when Logan had told her, at a party, that organized religion was a control system, and she had argued with him for an hour and gone home furious. She could not remember now which of them had been more certain, only that neither had known what they were talking about.

The prayer came late morning, the whole street folding itself into stillness. Laurie stood in the women's section beside her mother, and during a pause she saw, near the doors where the baskets stood, a family she did not recognize filling small bags with rice and dates, unhurried, unhunted by anyone's gaze. Nobody supervised them. Nobody signed anything. She found she was thinking about her own certainty, the kind she had defended to Logan years ago, and how it felt different from this, from watching a system work by simply being believed in.

Afterward, the street reopened like a hand unclenching. Children ran between the tables with foil-wrapped coins. Antonin asked whether the charity was given on Eid day itself, and Laurie said before the prayer, that was the whole point, the giving had to arrive in time to matter. Then she hesitated, because she was not sure she had that right either, whether it was the letter of it or her own preference for the shape of it, a deadline with a reason behind it. She said so out loud, which surprised her.

"You're allowed to not know," Antonin said. "I've been not knowing for months. It's very freeing."

She laughed, and then found herself telling him about the eighth envelope, the cousin, the arithmetic done in someone else's silence. She had decided, sitting there with the envelopes, that counting him was generosity, and now, saying it in daylight with the smell of grilled meat and rosewater all around them, she was not sure. Maybe generosity that decided for someone was just arithmetic with better lighting. Maybe it was fine. She had changed her mind twice since breakfast and suspected she would change it again before dinner, and that this was not a failure of conviction but something more like weather.

Her mother appeared at the edge of the crowd, waving, holding out a plate of dates toward the cousin's family, who were eating near the mosque steps, the small bags of rice tucked under the mother's arm like loaves. The cousin saw Laurie and raised a hand, and Laurie raised hers back, holding it there a moment longer than a greeting required.

"Come on," she said to Antonin, and started across the street toward them.

fact: One month of free rent on a twelve-month lease at 1,200 dollars a month lowers the effective monthly rent to 1,100 dollars.
story:
Lauren had folded the two lease printouts into quarters and then into eighths, so that opening them at the bus stop took a kind of patience, smoothing the creases against her knee while the October wind kept trying to take the top page. The Number 14 was late again. She had the schedules memorized by now, which was part of the problem, because she was trying to leave.

"Read it to me again," Sonya said. She was sitting on the bench with her backpack between her feet, chin on her fists. "The cheap one."

"Eleven fifty a month, utilities not included. On Grant Street." Lauren held the page at an angle so the streetlight caught it. "The other one's the Tower building. Twelve hundred, but they're running a move-in special. One month free."

Sonya snorted. "Free. Nothing's free."

"That's what my mom said. That's what everybody says, and then nobody says anything after that, which is why I'm doing this." Lauren took out her phone and opened the calculator, then closed it, then opened it again, because the wind was making the screen jump between apps as though the phone itself were undecided.

She had started this three days ago, after the fight. Her mother thought she should take the Grant Street apartment because it was cheaper, end of sentence, and when Lauren asked cheaper by how much, after utilities, after everything, her mother had said that questions like that were how people talked themselves into mistakes. Lauren had gone upstairs and made a spreadsheet. The spreadsheet was recalcitrant; every time she fixed the electric estimate, the water estimate looked wrong, and she had stayed up until one in the morning feeling like the numbers were arguing with her on purpose.

"Okay," she said now, working it aloud because Sonya was the only person who would sit through it. "The Tower is twelve hundred a month, twelve-month lease. One month free, so over the whole year I pay for eleven months. Eleven times twelve hundred." She typed. "Thirteen thousand two hundred. Divide by twelve, because that's what it actually costs me per month, spread out. Eleven hundred."

Sonya looked up. "So the free month makes it less than the cheap place."

"By fifty dollars. Before utilities." Lauren sat back against the bench. "Fifty dollars, and the Tower includes water and trash, and Grant Street includes nothing."

"So take the Tower. Done. Why do you look like that?"

Lauren didn't answer right away. A man across the street was trying to parallel park a van, pulling forward and back, forward and back, and she watched him until he gave up and drove on. The obvious move was to feel triumphant. She had caught the trick that everyone warned her about, the fine print that was supposed to beguile her, and turned it in her hand until it paid her. But the feeling that kept arriving instead was smaller and colder: if the special worked out to eleven hundred a month, why had the building written twelve hundred on the lease? Who was the free month really for? Maybe for people like her, who could do arithmetic and would feel clever and sign. Maybe for people who couldn't and would just see free.

"There's a version where I'm being smart," she said, "and a version where I'm being flattered. I can't tell which one I'm in."

"That's very you," Sonya said, not unkindly.

"I mean it. My mom sees a trap. Ms. Lombardi would see a deal, she told our whole econ class to calculate effective cost, she'd love this. And both of them are right about the world in general. The number is right, I've checked it four times. What I can't check is what the number is hiding." Lauren folded the pages, then unfolded the bottom one again, the Tower's, because there was one line she kept returning to: utilities included except electric, tenant pays electric, estimated usage not provided. "Estimated usage not provided. That's the part that could eat the fifty dollars, and I can't know it until I live there."

"So you're saying you don't know."

"I'm saying I know one thing exactly and everything else approximately, and I have to decide anyway." She heard how it sounded, like something from a college brochure, and Sonya was grinning at her, and Lauren laughed despite herself. "Fine. Yes. I don't know. I'm going to be the person who doesn't know things in a very organized way."

Far down the block, the 14 appeared, its lit sign floating above the traffic like something patient. Sonya stood and shouldered her backpack. "Ask them for a year of electric bills from the last tenant," she said. "Braedon did that when his brother moved. They had to go find them."

Lauren looked at her. "They'd actually show me?"

"Ask and see." The bus sighed against the curb and knelt, and the doors folded open, exhaling warm air that smelled of rain and vinyl. Sonya climbed the steps, tapped her pass, and turned. "Text me the number. The real one, after electric."

"I'll text you the number I have," Lauren said, "and then in January I'll text you the one I find out."

She got on, took the seat behind Sonya, and set the folded pages on her lap where the window's draft could reach them and ruffle the edges, the Tower's on top, its twelve hundred visible in the fold, the eleven fifty beneath it, both of them still, for eleven more minutes of riding, equally true.
