fact: In the United States, a new employee fills out Form W-4 so the employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck.
story:
The laminated menu above the register had a grease shine that no amount of wiping could remove, and Naomi stood beneath it in her interview clothes, feeling overdressed among the customers in their flip flops. Mr. Katz came out from the back wiping his hands on his apron, looked her up and down once, and said she could start Saturday if she could work weekends and holidays. That was the whole interview. She had prepared answers about teamwork that she now had no use for, and the absence of questions felt like a trick she hadn't figured out yet.

"Most kids quit in three weeks," he said, sliding a folder across the counter. "The fries do that. You acclimate or you don't." He tapped the folder. "Paperwork. Bring it back Saturday, filled out."

In the corner booth, Kyla was waiting with two milkshakes she hadn't paid for, having charmed the cashier into "samples." Kyla worked at the shoe store in the same strip and considered herself an authority on first jobs, dispensing advice with the trenchant confidence of someone who had held exactly one. Naomi opened the folder on the table between them. Inside was a packet, and on top of the packet a single sheet with lines and boxes, dense as a tax code, because that was more or less what it was.

"What is this," Naomi said. It wasn't a question so much as an objection.

Kyla leaned over, sucking audibly through her straw. "Oh, that. Dawson said it took him an hour. He put zero in every box just to be safe, and then his dad yelled at him about it." She went back to her shake. "Something about the government deciding how much it keeps."

Naomi read the first lines, and then read them again. The form wanted to know things she had never been asked: not whether she was honest or punctual, but a whole accounting of herself, her family, who else claimed her. She thought of her father filling out forms at the kitchen table in March, his jaw set, the calculator's tape curling onto the floor. She had never asked what any of it meant. It had seemed like weather, something adults stood outside in while she stayed indoors.

She photographed the form and sent it to her mother with a question mark, then a second text: "what do I put." The phone sat face up between the shakes. Kyla was explaining the fry station's hierarchy, how the drive-thru people thought they were better than everyone, and Naomi was nodding along while watching the screen. She texted Dawson too, since he had survived this exact form, and he answered fast, in his way: "no clue i guessed lol."

Her mother's reply came fourteen minutes later, which was fast, which was itself information Naomi would not process until later. "Put single and one allowance. I just did mine for the new job. Same form." Naomi read it three times. Her mother had a new job. Her mother had lost the old one, then, sometime between the winter and now, without a word of it reaching her, and this fact sat underneath the paperwork like a floor under a rug. She thought of the last four months of dinners, the smaller grocery runs, her mother laughing too easily at things that weren't jokes. Her mother's job had been as constant as the house.

"That form," Kyla said, watching her face. "Is it bad?"

"It's a Form W-4," Naomi said slowly, reading the top of the page. "You fill it out so they know how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck." She said it out loud mostly to fix it in her own mind, and it worked, the sentence assembling itself into something with edges. Each paycheck. Her paycheck. Money that would leave before it ever arrived, quietly, for reasons that were both hers and not hers.

"I don't get why they can't just take the same amount from everybody," Kyla said, and Naomi didn't get it either, not fully. She understood that the form was a way of telling the truth about yourself to a system that would otherwise guess, and that guessing wrong cost somebody something, though she couldn't have said who or how much. What she knew was that her mother, three weeks into a new job she had hidden from her daughter, had answered the same questions at some kitchen table, probably late at night, probably alone.

She copied the allowances her mother had told her onto the line, checked the box marked single, and signed her name in the blue pen Kyla handed her. Then she closed the folder and squared it on the table, one corner aligned with the edge, and took a long pull of the melting shake. Her phone buzzed once more. She turned it over and read, "proud of you," and set it face down again, and looked out the window at the parking lot where her bus would come.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: Jeremy Bentham's 1791 panopticon was a prison design with a central tower from which inmates could be watched at any time without knowing whether they were.
story:
The essay was due at 11:59, and at 9:40 Rose still had four hundred words to go, but she could not stop looking at the green dot beside her webcam. It had been lit since she logged into the scholarship portal, a small eye that came with the proctoring software the foundation required. It recorded her while she wrote. It flagged anything it decided was suspicious: a glance away, a voice in the room, a face the algorithm found too dark to read.

Erica had been flagged last month. That was the part Rose kept circling back to, the way Erica had said it on the phone, flat and tired: "It couldn't find my face in the lighting in my room, so it marked me for review. My essay was fine, but the review takes two weeks and the deadline doesn't." Erica had demurred when Rose asked if she'd fought it. She needed the scholarship more than she needed to be right, she said, and Rose hadn't known what to say to that.

At 10:15 she opened the chat with Cherish, who had already submitted the night before.

"Is the camera thing freaking you out too?" Rose typed.

"Girl, I sat perfectly still for three hours. Didn't get water, didn't look at my phone. Ms. Chen would've thought I was possessed."

Rose noticed she had been doing the same thing. Her neck ached. She had stopped talking to herself, which was how she usually thought her way through an ending. She had even muted her mother in the next room, waving her off mid-sentence, terrified of a second voice in the audio. Some invisible rulebook had installed itself in her body without her permission.

She typed, "ms chen gave us that handout about the prison guy"

"the panopticon," Cherish wrote back.

Rose scrolled through her downloads until she found it. "Jeremy Bentham's 1791 panopticon was a prison design with a central tower," she read aloud to the empty room, quietly, in case the microphone was listening, "from which inmates could be watched at any time without knowing whether they were." Bentham's trick wasn't watching everyone. It was making everyone believe they might be watched, so they'd watch themselves. She looked at the green dot. The tower didn't need guards anymore. It needed a webcam and a EULA nobody read.

She started typing faster. Her thesis had been about algorithmic bias, sourced and careful, but now the argument was turning into something more personal, something about how the machine didn't have to be right, it only had to be believed. At 11:20 she was two paragraphs from done when a banner appeared across the top of the screen. Review pending. Your session has been flagged for anomalous behavior. Beneath it, small and turbid with legalese, a notice that flagged submissions could be rescinded if the review found misconduct, and that the review process was confidential and could not be appealed by the applicant.

She called Erica. "Mine just got flagged. What did yours actually say?"

"Check your file status," Erica said. "Mine said 'face detection confidence low.' That's all. They never tell you the moment they flagged, so you don't know what you did. That's the whole point, Rose. You start guessing. You start apologizing for things you might not have done."

Rose checked. Hers said only: behavioral anomaly, timestamp 9:47. Which was nothing. Which was before she'd written a word, when she'd been staring at the green dot, deciding how still to sit. The clock in the corner read 11:34.

She could submit as is, flagged, and let an anonymous reviewer watch her recording and judge her pauses. Or she could close the portal, let the deadline pass, and email the foundation in the morning to ask whether a flagged session could be retaken, knowing from Erica that the answer was a two-week review and a closed window.

"There's no good denouement," she said to Erica. "Either way they win the argument, because either way I perform for the tower."

"You have twenty minutes," Erica said.

Rose looked at the unfinished essay, at the cursor blinking in the white field, at the green dot that would keep glowing whether she finished or not. Her mother opened the door with a cup of tea, and Rose, without thinking, raised a finger to her lips.

"Shh," she said. "It might hear you."

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Fat bloom is a dull grey or white streaky film that appears on chocolate that was not properly tempered or has melted and reset.
story:
The folding table outside the tent wobbled on its aluminum legs, and Rosalie steadied it with a flat stone from the fire ring before she set the bowl of chocolate down. Ms. Flores had said the site would be the whole point: no kitchen, no thermometer she trusted, only a pot of water, a bowl of melted chocolate, and whatever the wrist could feel. Rosalie had wanted to learn this since February, when she had watched a video at two in the morning and thought, briefly, that a person who could make chocolate snap cleanly could probably do anything.

Braiden had volunteered to be what he called quality control, which so far meant eating the failures. He sat on the cooler with a bag of pretzels and the expression of someone prepared to be very brave about upcoming disappointment. Aicha had brought the chocolate, a munificent three bars of the good stuff, because her mother had a rule about never traveling without real food. "If we ruin all of it," Aicha said, "I want you to understand that this was a personal gift, not a raw material."

Rosalalie stirred. The method Ms. Flores had shown her was seeding: melt most of the chocolate, then beat in chopped unmelted bits until the whole bowl cooled to a temperature you could not name but could, supposedly, feel against your inner lip. It was a strange way to learn something. Every instruction was a sensation with no number attached. She had spent four years of chemistry class being trained to distrust exactly this, to pathologize any measurement that came down to "you'll know it when you see it," and now she was supposed to dip a fingertip and decide.

She knew what failure looked like, at least. Her mother had once left a box of chocolates on the dashboard of the car through an August afternoon, and when Rosalie opened the box at the trailhead the pieces were streaked with a dull grey film, pale and white in places, like frost that had gotten bored halfway through. She had assumed the chocolate was ruined, expired, somehow spoiled, and had said so with real teenage conviction. It was Aicha, that same day, who had glanced over and said, "That's fat bloom. It happens when chocolate isn't tempered right, or when it melts and resets." Then Aicha had eaten one, which had settled the question of whether it was ruined more effectively than any argument could have.

Rosalie had thought about that for a long time afterward, the gap between ruined and merely wrong. The bloomed chocolate had tasted the same. The streaks were only a record of what heat had done, honest as a receipt. But it looked wrong, and looking wrong was, in the world she was about to enter, its own category of problem. She had been accepted to two colleges, one of which kept sending her emails with the word "branding" in them, and she had been trying since to work out which of her instincts were principles and which were just preferences about shine.

"Your lip," Braiden said, interrupting a reverie she had not noticed she was in. "You're staring at the bowl like it insulted you."

She dabbed a fingertip against the chocolate and touched it to her lip. Barely warm. Cooler than skin, which was the direction she wanted, she thought, or hoped, which amounted to the same thing in a campsite without a thermometer. She laid a strip of foil on the table, poured a thin puddle, and dragged the back of a spoon through it the way the video had shown. The chocolate moved like something that had opinions. She set the foil on the cooler's shady side and did not watch it, because Braiden was watching it for both of them and narrating under his breath.

Five minutes later it had set. She broke a corner off and held it up, and the break was clean, and the surface threw back the late light in a way that made even Braiden stop chewing. Aicha took the other half, snapped it near her ear on purpose, and looked so pleased with herself that Rosalie decided not to mention it.

The problem arrived after dinner, when the fire had gone down and the air off the lake turned cool. The remaining bowl of chocolate, covered with foil against the bugs, had been sitting too near the fire ring, and when Rosalie peeled the foil back the surface had gone soft and then, as it firmed in the evening air, streaked over with the same dull grey she knew from the dashboard box. She stood there holding the bowl and considering it. She could retemper the whole thing, seed it again, feel for the temperature one more time, and it would come back shiny. Or she could leave it, and it would taste exactly the same and look like evidence. Both were true at once, and the second was easier, and the first was the whole reason she had brought three bars' worth of a friend's generosity into the woods.

She picked up the spatula and the last of the chopped seeds.

"Again?" Braiden said.

"It's not ruined," Rosalie said. "It's just wrong." She stirred.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: According to the CDC, US drivers aged 16 to 19 have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged 20 and older, per mile driven.
story:
Noah had been waiting for the driving school's front office to open for eleven minutes, and in that time he had read the poster on the wall four times. It sat between a framed photo of a graduation class and a corkboard of coupons, and it said that according to the CDC, US drivers aged 16 to 19 have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged 20 and older, per mile driven. The first time he read it, the numbers had seemed abstract. By the fourth, they felt personal in a way he could not have defended if anyone had asked him to.

Adrianna came in behind him, shaking rain off her jacket. "You're before me on the list," she said. "Dang takes the six o'clock student first."

"I know."

"You've read that poster like it owes you money."

"It kind of does." He tapped the word fatal with one finger. "Per mile driven. So it's not just that we drive more. It's per mile."

Adrianna leaned in, read it once, and pulled a face. "That's a cheerful thing to put where we wait for our permit tests."

"Tell me about it." He wanted to say something else, something about how the fact sat in him like a stone, but Simeon arrived then, stamping wet shoes, carrying the energy of a person who had never once imagined dying in a car.

Simeon read the poster over their shoulders in four seconds. "Statistics," he said, with the confidence of someone burnishing his own composure. "You can make numbers say anything. It's specious, honestly. They want us scared so we pay for extra lessons."

"It's the CDC," Adrianna said. "Not an ad."

"Everything's an ad if you're cynical enough." Simeon grinned. "Come on. Being scared makes you worse at stuff. That's basically physics."

Mr. Dang appeared in the doorway to the lot, clipboard under his arm, keys in his fist. "Noah. You're up." He had a mannerism of pausing before the student's name, as if matching the face to a file, and it did nothing to calm Noah's pulse. "First lesson is parking lot only. We go out on the road when I say so, not before."

The car smelled like vinyl and air freshener shaped like a pine tree. Noah adjusted the mirror three times because twice did not seem like enough. His hands on the wheel were exactly where the poster in his head said ten and two, and he was aware of being aware of it, which he suspected was its own kind of mistake.

"Foot on brake. Start it." The engine turned over. "Now let it creep. No gas. Just steer."

The car rolled forward, enormous and quiet, and Noah understood immediately that he had been thinking about driving as a skill, like typing, when it was actually a negotiation. The car wanted to continue. Everything about its mass said so. He steered around the first cone and clipped the second, a soft plastic knock that made his ears hot.

"You're looking at the cone," Mr. Dang said. "Look where you want to go."

"It's a cone."

"It's practice for a kid on a bicycle." The sentence landed without any softening at all, and Noah did the next loop with his eyes far ahead, and the wheels missed everything. He could hear Simeon's voice in his head calling the poster specious, and it was true that fear had made his first loop worse. But it was also true that he was sixteen, and the paper on the wall had not been an opinion. Both things could be real at once. He could not fully square them, and he decided, gripping the wheel through the next turn, that he was not required to.

"Better," Mr. Dang said. "Now park between the two white lines. Slow, slow, stop."

Noah parked. It was crooked but inside the lines, and he sat with his foot on the brake, breathing, while rain ticked on the roof. Through the windshield he could see Adrianna at the window of the office, reading the poster again, mouthing the words. Per mile driven, her lips shaped.

"Question," Noah said. "That statistic on your wall. The one about sixteen to nineteen. Do you believe it, or is it just there to scare us?"

Mr. Dang looked at him for a long moment, then out at the wet lot, the cones, the rain going silver in the sodium light. "It's there because it's true," he said. "Scared is not the point. Careful is the point."

"Adrianna's taking her permit test after me," Noah said. "Should I tell her the numbers, or just let her drive?"

"That," said Mr. Dang, and shifted the clipboard on his knee, "is not my question to answer. Reverse us out. Slow."

Noah found the gear, checked the mirror twice because once did not seem like enough, and let the car glide backward into the rain.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: Aristotle held that people are responsible for actions done voluntarily, and that actions done under force or through ignorance of the circumstances can be involuntary.
story:
Dinner was pork chops and the good rice, the kind his mother only made when she wanted the table to feel like a place where things got said. Noah pushed his chop around the plate and waited for his father to ask, because his father always asked, and tonight Noah almost wanted him to.

"How was school," his father said, not a question so much as a formality, his eyes still on his phone until his mother cleared her throat and the phone went face-down on the counter behind him.

"Somebody got hurt," Noah said. "Not physically. There's this guy, Alexandre. He makes these study guides, really good ones, and he'd started to monetize them, like a dollar a download, saving up for engineering school. And a week ago somebody started saying he'd copied most of the guides off paid course materials nobody our age can even access." He cut a piece of pork he didn't eat. "Today Ms. Malik got an email from some teacher at another school. The guides are clean. He wrote them. Somebody just decided he couldn't have."

His mother set down her fork. "So he's cleared. That's something."

"He's cleared and nobody believes it the same way. The downloads stopped. He walked into the cafeteria today and a table went quiet." Noah could still see it, Alexandre standing there with his tray, deciding in the space of two seconds whether to sit anyway, and sitting anyway, truculent, chin up, staring at his food like it had insulted him. "And here's the part I keep chewing on. The rumor got big because Bianca repeated it. She's in my ethics class. She heard it from a girl on her bus and she put it in the group chat with a question mark after it, like, is this true? And then forty people forwarded it without the question mark."

"So she started it," his father said.

"She spread it. She didn't start it." Noah heard how defensive he sounded and kept going anyway. "We just did this reading. Aristotle. He held that people are responsible for actions done voluntarily, and that actions done under force or through ignorance of the circumstances can be involuntary." He said the last word carefully, the way he'd underlined it twice in his notebook. "So if Bianca had known it was false and passed it on anyway, that's on her, completely. But she didn't know. She was ignorant of the circumstances. By Aristotle's logic, that part of it is involuntary."

His mother tilted her head. "That's very tidy for a girl who wrecked someone's business with one text."

"That's what I keep running into." He described it as best he could, the thing Ms. Malik had written on the board when a kid asked how anyone can know anything for sure: epistemology, the study of knowledge itself, what you can claim to know and how. "Bianca's defense is she didn't know. But Aristotle also has this idea that some ignorance is your own fault. Like if you didn't check because checking was inconvenient. She never asked Alexandre. She never asked the girl on the bus where she heard it. She asked the group chat, which is the one place guaranteed not to have an answer." He paused. "So is that voluntary or not? Choosing not to know. Is that still ignorance of the circumstances, or is it something you did on purpose?"

"Does she feel bad?" his mother asked.

"She skipped fifth period. Alexandre's sister found her behind the gym and she wouldn't come inside." He thought of Bianca at lunch the day after the text, laughing at something, not yet knowing what she'd set in motion, and then yesterday, her hands shoved in her sleeves, walking the long way past his locker so she wouldn't have to nod at him. The unintended consequences part was what staggered him. A question mark, forty forwards, a silent cafeteria. Nobody had chosen any of it, and it had all happened anyway.

"There's a assembly thing tomorrow," he said. "Ms. Malik opened class today saying the floor was ours if anyone wanted it. Alexandre's going to stand up and read the email, I think. He asked me this afternoon if I'd say something about Bianca. Like, that she's not the same as whoever made it up." He looked at his plate. "I told him I'd think about it. And I have been. Because I can hold both things, I think. She didn't do it voluntarily in the way Aristotle means, and she still should have checked, and Alexandre still lost two weeks of money and every lunch period. All three of those can be true. What I can't figure out is what to actually say tomorrow that does any good without making it sound like I'm grading her guilt in front of everyone."

His father picked his phone back up, turned it over, and set it down again without looking at it. "You could ask her what she wants said."

Noah sat with that while his mother took his plate and stacked it on hers. It was so obvious it was almost insulting, and also the one thing he hadn't considered, because he'd been so busy ranking blames that he hadn't thought to ask the person carrying them. He got his jacket from the hook by the door, and his mother called after him to be back before ten, and he was already texting Bianca as he stepped out onto the porch: Can I come by for five minutes?

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, every new employee must complete Section 1 of Form I-9, which verifies identity and permission to work, no later than their first day of paid work.
story:
The fluorescent lights of Henderson's Grocery made everything look slightly underwater, and Kaylee stood at the customer service desk clutching a folder the assistant manager had handed her ten minutes earlier. Inside was a schedule for orientation, a laminated sheet about produce codes, and a form she had never seen before, printed on both sides, with a title in small government letters. She was supposed to start work at four o'clock. It was already three-forty.

"You look like you're reading a tax audit," said Lorelai, who had biked over after cross-country practice to watch Kaylee's first day, mostly out of curiosity and partly because she had applied to the same store and not heard back. Lorelai picked up a display of discount candy and put it down again. "What is that thing?"

"It says Form I-9." Kaylee turned the page over, then back. "Section 1. It wants to know if I'm a citizen, or a permanent resident, or something else, and there's a line for my Social Security number only if my employer uses E-Verify, which I don't know if they do." She said the words slowly, like she was translating as she went. "It says every new employee has to complete Section 1 no later than their first day of paid work." She checked her phone. "Which is in eighteen minutes."

Lorelai leaned against the desk. "So fill it out. You have a Social Security card, right?"

"My mom has it. In a fireproof box." Kaylee's stomach did something complicated. All week she had been turning the job over in her mind, less as money than as proof: proof that she could show up somewhere new, unaccompanied, and be useful. She had imagined bagging groceries with brisk competence. She had not imagined paperwork with deadlines, or the possibility that she would stand here at four o'clock with an incomplete form and be sent home, back to being a person who had never worked anywhere.

Talon appeared from aisle three, where he had worked since September, pushing a train of carts with one hand and eating a granola bar with the other. He was in her grade but she barely knew him; he existed in the category of people who had already crossed over into having jobs and paychecks. "Mori's on shift," he said, nodding toward the registers. "She'll tell you what to bring."

Ms. Mori had taught Kaylee's older cousin chemistry years ago and now, apparently, worked the express lane on weekends. When Kaylee approached with the form, Ms. Mori glanced at it and then at her, and something like recognition passed across her face. "First job," she said. It wasn't a question.

"I can't finish Section 1 without my card," Kaylee said. "Or maybe I can, there's a box that says I don't need the number unless something called E-Verify, and I don't know what we are." She heard her own voice getting faster. "And the sheet says no later than my first day of paid work, which is today, so if I don't finish it today then I can't be paid today, or I can't work today, or both, and my mom's at her shift until eleven."

Ms. Mori scanned a carton of eggs and slid it down the belt. "Do you have a passport? License?" When Kaylee shook her head, the earlier malaise, which had been sitting in her chest like weather, began to transmute into something more like urgency, and also, unexpectedly, clarity. She wasn't helpless; she had a phone, a bus route, and a mother who answered texts even during doubles. She stepped away from the register and called, and her mom picked up on the second ring, and after a long pause said she kept a photocopy of the card in the folder by the microwave, and that Kaylee's brother was home and could photograph it.

The photograph arrived blurry. The second one arrived clear. At four-twelve, Kaylee stood at the customer service desk with the assistant manager, who looked at the image on her phone, then at Section 1, and told her to fill it out and bring the original within the week for Section 2. She wrote her name in the small boxes, one letter per box, checking the citizen box with a pen that left a noxious chemical smell, the kind that made her nose sting. Behind her, Lorelai bought a pack of gum with exact change and said, "One of these days that'll be you ringing me up."

"Maybe Tuesday," Kaylee said. She signed her name at the bottom, then slid the form across the desk and reached for the apron folded on top of the register.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: To indemnify someone is to promise, in a contract, to compensate them for losses they suffer because of certain acts, often written alongside a promise to 'hold harmless'.
story:
The gym smelled of rubber mats and disinfectant, and the man behind the front desk slid a clipboard across the counter before Joshua had finished saying why he'd come. He wanted the multipurpose room on a Saturday evening, three hours, for a charity tournament his class was running. Hubert had organized the brackets, Alexa had designed the posters, and twenty-six people had already paid five dollars each to enter. The room was forty dollars. It should have been simple.

"Read the terms and conditions," the desk man said. "Initial the boxes. Signature at the bottom, page three."

Joshua read. Most of it was ordinary: no tape on the walls, no food outside the lobby, rental fees nonrefundable within forty-eight hours. Then, on page two, a paragraph in denser print caught him. The renter agreed to release the gym from all liability for injury or property damage, and further agreed to indemnify and hold harmless the gym, its owners and employees, against any claims arising from the renter's use of the premises.

He read it twice. The word indemnify sat there like a locked door.

"You're blocking the line," Hubert said behind him. An older man waiting to buy a day pass had begun to make a querulous sound in his throat, the noise of someone assembling a complaint, and the desk man glanced over Joshua's shoulder with a flat, patient face that suggested this happened hourly.

"One second." Joshua stepped aside, took out his phone, and photographed the paragraph. He texted it to Alexa, who was meeting them in ten minutes with the poster tube and the cash box. Then he stood by the water fountain and worked through what he could. Release from liability, he understood; that was the gym saying if you get hurt, don't sue us. But indemnify was something else, something that ran in the opposite direction. He could feel the shape of it without seeing it whole.

Alexa arrived, read her phone, then the paper itself, her finger under the line. "My cousin does event insurance," she said. "To indemnify someone is to promise, in a contract, to compensate them for losses they suffer because of certain acts. It's usually written right next to hold harmless. So if somebody trips over our extension cord and sues the gym, we don't just lose; we pay for their side too."

"So it's not enough that we can't sue them," Joshua said. "We have to cover them if anyone else does."

"Basically."

Hubert, who had been listening with his arms folded, unfolded them. "It's a rec room in a gym, not a demolition site. Nobody's going to sue."

"Somebody's little brother twisted his wrist at the school bake sale last year," Alexa said. "His mom mentioned lawyers in the pickup lane for a month."

They argued about it in low voices by the pro shop. Hubert thought Joshua was turning one paragraph into a crisis, and said so; Joshua thought Hubert was choosing not to read, which was its own kind of signature. Alexa, typically, refused to pick a side and instead called her mother, who said something that made Alexa press the phone harder to her ear and then say "wait, say that again" twice. When she hung up, she looked between them. "Mom says small claims happen, and she's seen a gym go after a family once. Also she says I have to stop calling her at work."

Joshua went back to the counter. The querulous man was gone, and the desk man was restocking towels.

"I'm sixteen," Joshua said. "Can I even sign this?"

The desk man paused. "Signature of renter, and signature of parent or guardian. There's a line for both."

That settled part of it and unsettled the rest. His mother would sign; she signed his field trip forms without reading them, which was exactly what he had almost done. He understood the gym's side now, understood it well enough that he could defend it to Hubert later: they ran rooms for strangers, and strangers fell down, and the contract was how a business survived being vilified the first time somebody's wrist bent the wrong way. But he also understood that the language pressed all of the risk downward, onto whoever held the pen, and that the person holding the pen tonight was supposed to be him.

"I want the room," he said. "But I want to ask one thing first. If a guest gets hurt, and it's their own fault, does this still mean we pay?"

The desk man looked at the paragraph, then at Joshua, and for the first time seemed to actually see him. "Honest answer? Depends what the act was. The lawyers write it wide."

Joshua nodded. He spread the form flat on the counter, took out his phone again, and photographed every page, front desk, terms, conditions, the small print and the wide spaces for names. He texted his mother the photos with the message, read page two before you sign. Then he laid his own pen against the renter's line, and Alexa leaned in, and Hubert said, "Three hours, forty dollars, let's go," and Joshua began to write his name.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: A lawyer who types faster than her assistant still gains by hiring him to type, because every hour she spends typing is an hour of better-paid legal work given up.
story:
Laura had been running her math tutoring business out of the food court for six weeks, and it was starting to drown her. Five students, two of them Arthur's younger cousins, all of whom texted her at all hours to reschedule, and every Sunday night she spent forty minutes with a spreadsheet that she could have finished in twenty. Her brother, who was eleven and mercenary, had offered to handle the scheduling for four dollars a week and a cut of any new clients he recruited. Laura was faster at it. That was the part that bothered her, sitting there at the table between the pretzel stand and the fountain, because it seemed obvious that you should never pay someone to do something you did better.

She said as much to Zoe, who had arrived with an enormous iced coffee and no visible sympathy. "You spend your whole Sunday on this," Zoe said, tapping the spreadsheet, which Laura had opened on her phone under the table like something shameful. "You charge twenty dollars an hour for tutoring and you're doing eleven-year-old labor for free."

"It's not labor, it's a spreadsheet. It takes me twenty minutes."

"It takes your life," Zoe said. "It circumscribes your whole weekend. That's a real word, look it up." She stole a pretzel.

Laura was saved from arguing by the arrival of Arthur, who was carrying a shopping bag containing, he announced, an anachronistic film camera he'd found secondhand, because apparently the mall still had a shop for people who wanted to look artistic in 1994. He sat down, heard the argument in its entirety within about nine seconds, and held up a hand.

"Okay, my mom explained this to me once, it's from her econ class. There's this lawyer, right? She types faster than her assistant. Faster, fully, no contest. And she still hires him to type."

"That's stupid," Laura said. "She should type."

"Why?"

"Because she's better at it."

Arthur bit into his own pretzel with the patience of someone who had once made the same mistake. "Because every hour she spends typing is an hour of better-paid legal work given up. That's the whole thing. It's called comparative advantage. She's better at both, but she only gains from the one that pays more, so she trades."

Laura looked at her spreadsheet. Twenty dollars an hour for tutoring, four hours of Sunday scheduling that her brother would happily do for less than the price of two pretzels. "So I'm the lawyer," she said slowly, "and my brother is the assistant, and I've been typing."

"Congratulations," Zoe said. "It only took you six weeks and a bag of pretzel bites."

That night she offered her brother the job. He negotiated her up to six dollars a week and a signing bonus of one movie ticket, which Laura felt was extortion, and which he described as "market rate." He reorganized her calendar in rainbow colors, misspelled the word "Wedensday," and recruited a new client from his soccer team within three days, which was genuinely more than she had managed in a month. On Sunday she had her evening back, and she sat at her desk not knowing quite what to do with it, because the spreadsheet had become a habit, a small penance she'd been paying to no one. She started outlining a history essay instead, about reparations after a war, about how the accounting of who owes what never quite closes, and she thought briefly of her brother's six dollars and how she had been paying the wrong person all along.

The following week one of the soccer-team clients quit without paying, her brother forgot to tell her about a rescheduled session until she was already at the mall, and Laura stood by the fountain for a moment wanting, honestly, to fire him. Zoe, passing by with her enormous coffee, raised it in a small salute. Laura texted her brother instead: "You still up for Saturday? Same rate." Then she put the phone away and went to find the pretzel stand, because she'd promised to bring him one, and he'd earned it, mostly.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and people who do not vote without a valid reason can be fined.
story:
Justin had the ballot guide folded into quarters in his jacket pocket, and by the time he reached the counter at the coffee shop he had unfolded and refolded it twice since leaving home. He ordered a small black coffee and took the table by the window, where Hamza was already sitting with his laptop open and three empty sugar packets lined up beside the cup like casualties.

"You voted yet?" Hamza asked, without looking up.

"At four," Justin said. "My mother gets off work at three-thirty and she wants to go together. She's been talking about it all week like it's a graduation."

Hamza turned the laptop toward him. On the screen was a table of countries, voting systems, turnout percentages, built for the comparative politics paper that was due in November. "Look at this," Hamza said. "Australia. Compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925. You don't vote, you get fined, unless you have a valid reason."

"Seriously?" Justin leaned in. "They fine you?"

"A hundred-something dollars, I think. I didn't write the amount down because the paper's about turnout, not penalties. But yeah. Since 1925. You skip it and you pay."

Niko arrived then, shaking rain off his jacket, and dropped into the third chair before anyone invited him. He had opinions the way other people had loose change, and he spent them just as freely. "Fining people for not voting is insane," he said, having heard only the last exchange from the doorway. "It's a right, not a chore. If you don't care, that's the vote."

"It's a duty in Australia, apparently," Hamza said. "Different frame."

"It's coercion with paperwork," Niko said. He flagged the cashier and ordered a cappuccino with extra foam, then spent a moment watching the steam wand as though it owed him something. He wanted, Justin had noticed over four years of sharing classes with him, to be the person in any room who had already settled the question, and settled it more cleverly than everyone else.

Justin drank his coffee and looked out at the wet street. His own position, if he had one, was harder to say out loud. He had grown up on his mother's version of the vote, which was close to sacrament: her grandmother had walked miles to a polling station in a country where the result was already known, and the walking itself had been the point. Rectitude, she called it, though she pronounced it in her own accent, and the word had always carried weight in their kitchen. At the same time Justin had spent the autumn arguing with Hamza's older brother online, where people eviscerated each other over candidates they agreed with on nine issues out of ten, and it had made him wonder whether forced participation would produce conviction or only noise, a room where everyone must speak and nobody is heard. Both things felt true. He did not know how to hold them at once.

Mr. Santos, who taught history at the school two blocks over and came here every afternoon at four, stopped beside their table with his mug and nodded at Hamza's screen. "Australia?" he said. "Good paper topic." He did not stay to elaborate. He took his regular seat near the door and opened his newspaper, and Justin was oddly grateful; the last thing he needed was an adult handing him the conclusion.

"Here's what I don't get," Hamza said, scrolling. "Niko says compulsion ruins the principle. But the principle's supposed to be representation, right? And if a fifth of the country stays home, the representatives represent fewer people. So which principle wins?"

"The one where the state doesn't fine you for being bored," Niko said.

"Is that a principle or a mood?"

Niko's cappuccino arrived. He stirred it longer than it needed, and Justin could see him assembling a long answer, the kind Niko gave, prolix and studded with philosophers he had read half of. Justin cut across it before it could start.

"I don't think it's either," he said. "My mother votes like it's a debt she's paying forward. And I used to think that was just an old-person thing. But compulsory voting since 1925 means a whole country decided the debt is real enough to collect. I'm not saying I'd want the fine here. I'm saying maybe the two ideas aren't opposites. Maybe it's a right that some people treat as a duty, and the law just makes the duty explicit instead of leaving it to whoever had a grandmother who walked somewhere."

Hamza typed that, or something near it, without asking. Niko looked at Justin over the cup with the expression of a chess player watching someone move a piece he had forgotten about.

"So you're for it," Niko said.

"I'm for my mother walking me to the school gym at four o'clock," Justin said. "The rest I'm still deciding, and I've decided that's allowed."

He finished the coffee, left the cup on the saucer, and pulled the ballot guide from his pocket one last time. Outside, the rain had thinned to a drizzle, and his mother would be at the house by now, standing in the doorway with her coat already on.

"I have to go," he said, and buttoned his jacket. At the door he looked back and pointed at Hamza's laptop. "Put Australia in bold."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: In 2023, US workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma had median weekly earnings of $899, compared with $708 for those without one.
story:
The hallway outside the gym smelled like floor wax and lilies, and Elizabeth stood in it holding her cap in both hands as though it might blow away. She had graduated twenty minutes ago. The tassel kept swinging against her wrist.

Alek found her first, still in his gown, holding his phone up to take a picture before she could arrange her face. "You're not smiling," he said. "You look like you're being arraigned."

"I'm thinking."

"After the ceremony? That's a scheduling failure." He took the picture anyway.

Her uncle had said it at dinner the night before, over her mother's good plates. "You know what that diploma's worth?" he had asked, waving his fork. "In 2023, workers twenty-five and over with a high school diploma had median weekly earnings of $899. Without one, $708." He had leaned back, satisfied, as if he had personally handed her the difference. Her mother had told him not to aggrandize a piece of paper, and he had said he wasn't aggrandizing anything, he was quoting statistics, which was different, and Elizabeth had pushed her potatoes around her plate and said nothing. One hundred and ninety-one dollars a week. It was the first time anyone had put a number on what she'd done, and she hadn't decided yet whether the number honored it or diminished it.

Maximus came down the hallway with his gown unzipped and flapping, dragging his younger brother by the sleeve. "Lizzie. Lizzie, tell this child that college is real and he should be afraid."

"Tell him the numbers instead," Elizabeth said.

"What numbers?"

"High school diploma, twenty-five and over, median weekly earnings in 2023: $899. No diploma: $708." She heard her uncle's cadence come out of her mouth and winced at it.

Maximus's brother, who was thirteen and allergic to sincerity, said, "Cool, so I just have to not drop out and I get two hundred more dollars a week."

"It's $191 more," Elizabeth said. "And that's not what it means."

"Then what does it mean?"

She opened her mouth. This was the problem. She had been turning it over all night, the way the diploma in her hand was both a piece of pressed board and apparently a financial instrument, and she could not get the two things to lie flat together. "It means something," she said. "I'm working on what."

Ms. Joshi emerged from the gym doors with a stack of programs under her arm. She taught eleventh-grade history and had once told Elizabeth, during a unit on labor movements, that every statistic was a person standing very still. Elizabeth had written it in the margin of her notebook and then, later, underlined it, which was as close as she ever came to a religion.

"Elizabeth. I have an injunction for you." Ms. Joshi handed her a program; Elizabeth's name was on the second page, spelled correctly. "Do not let anyone tell you what today means. Not your uncle, not me, not a spreadsheet. The meaning is the one thing they can't issue you with the diploma."

"My uncle already tried," Elizabeth said. "He told me what it's worth."

"Ah. The famous $899."

"You know about that?"

"Everyone in the faculty room knows about that. Parents have been quoting it all week." Ms. Josji smiled, then didn't. "It's true, incidentally. Or true enough. But true things can still be equivocal, and I'd want you to sit with that instead of resolving it tonight." She gathered her programs more tightly. "Go find your mother. She's crying by the water fountain and pretending it's allergies."

Elizabeth walked down the hallway with the cap under her arm and the program rolled in her fist. Behind her, Maximus was still lecturing his brother, who was saying fine, fine, he'd stay in school, could they go get food now. Alek was showing the photo to a group of girls from her chemistry class, and one of them called out that Elizabeth looked like a philosopher, and Elizabeth thought, not for the first time, that the hallway was a strange place to have the last conversation of your childhood, under fluorescent lights, with a vending machine humming in the corner like a witness.

Here was what she had, so far. The diploma was worth $191 a week to someone twenty-five and older, which was not her yet, and which was a median anyway, which meant half the people were on the other side of it, and she did not know which half she would be. The diploma was also worth her mother's face at the water fountain, and Ms. Joshi's margin note, and four years of papers she had sometimes loved. Both of those were true. She could hold the market value and the other value at the same time without deciding which one counted more, and maybe that was not weakness in her thinking, maybe that was the whole of it: a considered position with an honest hole in the middle.

Her uncle was not a bad man. He wanted the best for her and the best, in his vocabulary, had a dollar figure attached. Her mother wanted something she couldn't name and got embarrassed when she tried. Ms. Joshi wanted her to refuse both offers, which was itself an offer, and Elizabeth noticed that too.

She found her mother by the fountain, dabbing at her eyes with a program.

"It's allergies," her mother said.

"I know." Elizabeth unrolled her own program and looked at her name again. Then she put the cap on her mother's head, tilted, and adjusted the tassel so it hung over one eye.

"There," she said. "Now we match."

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: Melvyn Leffler's A Preponderance of Power, which won the 1993 Bancroft Prize, argued US leaders pursued national security through dominance of the postwar world.
story:
Charlie's essay was due on Friday, and by Tuesday she had written the same paragraph four times. The prompt, printed at the top of Ms. García's handout, asked her to weigh two historians' explanations of the Cold War against the evidence, and so far her weighing amounted to describing one historian, then the other, then writing "however" between them. She was sitting in the school library with her shoes hooked on the rung of a chair, a stack of books nobody else had touched in weeks at her elbow.

Rory slid into the seat across from her and stole a pretzel from the bag she was guarding with her elbow. "Still on the nuclear thing?"

"It's not a thing, it's a question. Why did the Cold War happen the way it did." She turned the handout so he could read it. "I've got Gaddis. Gaddis says the Americans were reacting, mostly. Security, not conquest. But Ms. García said if I only use one historian I'm just doing a book report with extra steps."

"Gaddis is the one you already read?"

"Cover to cover, twice. I could recite him." She flattened her hand on the book's cover, and the gesture felt like a vow, or a surrender, she couldn't tell which.

Rory chewed and pointed his pretzel at the shelf behind her. "That one's been staring at you for an hour."

It was a thick blue volume, spine cracked at the middle where some previous senior had given up halfway. A Preponderance of Power, by Melvyn Leffler. She'd skimmed the first pages a week ago and set it aside because Gaddis was easier, because Gaddis had sentences she could underline and carry like evidence in her pocket. She pulled Leffler down now and read the copyright page, the way she'd been taught, hunting for the tell that a book mattered. There it was, on the jacket flap: the Bancroft Prize, 1993. She checked the front again, because a prize could be a printing error or a librarian's wishful sticker, but the flap was plain about it.

"Is that good?" Rory asked.

"It's the big one, for history. Bancroft, 1993." She said it quietly, the way you confirm a rumor you hope is true. Rory gave her a thumbs up and returned to his chemistry homework, and she settled into the argument.

The argument was this, as far as she could pull it out of four hundred dense pages before the bell: American leaders had gone after national security by trying to dominate the postwar world. Not by accident, not reluctantly, the way Gaddis sometimes implied, but as a policy. Leffler even used the word, and once she'd seen it she found it everywhere, surfacing in his sentences like a carp in a river. "Hegemony," she said aloud, testing it, and Rory looked up as if she'd sneezed.

On Thursday she stayed after for Ms. García's office hours, carrying both books and a legal pad covered in her worst handwriting. Max was already there, arguing about his own essay, and Charlie waited in the hallway listening to the hum of the vending machine until he came out looking defeated.

"Ms. García, I have a problem," Charlie said, sitting down. "Gaddis says the US was defending the world order. Leffler's book, A Preponderance of Power, it won the Bancroft Prize in 1993, it says they wanted dominance, that dominance was the security plan. So one of them is wrong, or I'm wrong."

"Or," Ms. García said, and stopped there, folding her hands, because she was the kind of teacher who believed in or.

Charlie looked at her legal pad. She had three columns: Gaddis, Leffler, and a middle column she'd labeled EVIDENCE and filled with things like the Marshall Plan, the atomic monopoly before 1949, the NSC-68 memo. The trouble was that the evidence refused to sit still. The Marshall Plan looked like aid from one angle and control from another, depending on which book she held it next to. The riparian metaphor she'd scrawled in the margin, thinking of the Iron Curtain countries as two banks of one river, each side claiming the water in the middle, only reminded her that a river belongs to whoever has the bigger pump.

"I think," she said slowly, "they're both describing the same thing and arguing about the word for it. Like, if you build a dam because you're afraid of floods, is that security or dominance? It's both, and the answer depends on whether the people downstream got a vote."

Ms. García's eyebrows moved, which was the most enthusiasm she ever showed. "And your essay says what, exactly?"

"That Leffler's right that the goal was preponderance, because the policy documents talk like that, but Gaddis is right about the fear, because the same documents are scared. And what I can't resolve, and I'm going to say I can't, is whether the fear caused the dominance or excused it." Charlie heard her own voice speed up and reeled it back. "I don't want to suture them together with some third paragraph that pretends they agree. I'd rather show the seam."

"Show the seam," Ms. García repeated. She wrote nothing down, which Charlie had learned meant the opposite of what it meant with other teachers. "Friday. Don't be late."

That night Charlie wrote until one in the morning, and when she finished, the essay's last paragraph admitted that a historian's choice of lens was itself a kind of evidence, and that she could not test the lenses against each other, only against the documents, and the documents spoke both languages at once. She emailed it, closed the laptop, and stood at her window watching the empty street. Somewhere in her backpack, the blue book was due back at the library on Monday. She decided she would renew it instead, and went to find a granola bar.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: The relational model of databases was introduced by IBM researcher Edgar F. Codd in a 1970 paper, 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks'.
story:
The library had a smell of warm carpet and returned paperbacks, and Robert claimed the computer nearest the window before anyone else could, sliding his notebook flat beside the keyboard. On the screen was the practice database Mr. Malik had set up for the coding club: two tables, Customers and Orders, full of invented names and invented purchases. The assignment was printed on a half sheet. Find the customers who have never ordered anything. Robert had been staring at it for two days.

Slade dropped into the chair beside him with a can of soda he was not supposed to have indoors and peered at the half sheet. "So just, like, look through the customers and check."

"There are four thousand rows," Robert said. "And next week it'll be a million."

"Then it's a bad assignment."

Marcel arrived a minute later, hair still damp from gym, and set his own notebook down on Robert's other side without asking, which was how the three of them worked. He read the problem, then read it again, then said, "You can't just ask for rows that aren't there. A query gives you what's in the tables."

"That's the whole thing," Robert said. "I'm asking the database about absence."

He typed his first attempt, a join between the two tables with a condition, and ran it. The result came back as every customer who had ordered something, which was the opposite of the problem, four hundred rows of people happily spending money. He tried adding a condition on the Orders side, some way of saying "where the order is nothing," and got an empty set. The machine sat there, serene, giving him exactly what he'd asked for and nothing he wanted.

Mr. Malik passed behind them on his slow circuit of the room, shelf-read a few spines, and paused. "Stuck?"

"I'm trying to join to find people who didn't order," Robert said.

"Think about what a join actually does when one side has no match," Mr. Malik said, and moved on, which was his way; he answered questions with smaller questions and seemed to think this was generous, and mostly it was.

Robert leaned back and stared at the ceiling tiles. Marcel had gone quiet in the way he did when a problem interested him, and Slade had wandered off toward the magazines. The window gave onto the parking lot, where a woman was loading her trunk with what looked like an entire small library of her own, and Robert watched her without seeing her. Tables. Why was any of this made of tables? Somebody had to have decided that. He pulled up the encyclopedia terminal, because the club computers were blocked from the regular internet, and typed in relational database.

The entry gave him a name. Edgar F. Codd, a researcher at IBM, who introduced the relational model in a 1970 paper called "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks." Robert read the title twice. Data banks, not databases; the language of a time when the idea itself was new. Codd had decided, or argued, that data should live in these flat grids, related to each other by shared values, and everything Robert had been fighting all afternoon was downstream of that one decision, made before he was born, by someone he'd never heard of. He read the line aloud, quietly, just the title, and Marcel leaned over.

"Seventy pages?" Marcel said, mishearing.

"Nineteen seventy. The year."

"It's an epigram, almost," Marcel said. "The title, I mean. It tells you everything in one line. Tables relating to tables." He tapped the screen. "So if the whole model is about relations, then the missing people have to be a relation too. The join has to be able to say 'no relation.'"

Robert sat forward. A join kept the rows that matched. There was a form of join, he half remembered from the notes, that kept everything from one side whether it matched or not, and left the other side empty where there was no match. He typed it out, left join, Customers to Orders, and then the condition: where the order's customer number is null. Not empty, the way he'd tried before, but null, the database's way of saying the other table simply had nothing to offer. He ran it.

The result filled the screen below the query: one hundred and six rows. Names, addresses, no orders. Robert counted the first ten with his finger, then checked three of them against the Orders table by hand, one at a time, and each search came back empty. They had really never bought anything. It had worked, and it had worked by letting the join fail on purpose, by asking for the gap itself.

Slade came back with a magazine about motorcycles. "Solved it?"

"Six ways to be wrong and one way to be right," Robert said. He copied the query into his notebook in careful print, then, underneath, wrote the year 1970 and Codd's name, because it seemed rude not to. He was still not entirely sure he understood why null meant what it meant, whether it was absence or something stranger, and he underlined the word and left it that way.

Marcel was already altering the query, dropping in an extra condition, intransigent about testing whether it held under pressure. "Make a customer with an order that was cancelled," he said. "If they show up in your list, the answer's wrong."

"Then I'll find out," Robert said, and reached for the keyboard.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The 1987 Montreal Protocol, which phases out ozone-destroying chemicals, was the first treaty in United Nations history to be ratified by every UN member state.
story:
Samuel arrived at the community garden on Delancey Street with a plastic bag of seed potatoes and a debate brief folded into his back pocket, and he was not sure which of the two mattered more to him. The debate was Monday: countries can never agree on an environmental problem, he was assigned to argue the affirmative, and his partner Tyrell had texted him three links that all said the same discouraging thing. The potatoes were for the plot Ms. Popescu had assigned him in April, back when the garden was still mostly mud and he had signed up mostly because his mother thought it would look good on applications.

Tyrell was already there, kneeling in the bed by the fence, pulling weeds with the distracted violence of someone whose mind was somewhere else. He looked up when Samuel dropped the bag. "You find anything yet? Anything we can actually use?"

"Not yet," Samuel said, which was true in the way that half-truths are true. He had spent Saturday in the library and had copied down a paragraph from an encyclopedia, but he had not read it closely, and there was a folded corner on the page he did not want to unfold in front of Tyrell and get wrong.

They worked for a while in the noise of the neighborhood, which was its own kind of argument: a bus on Delancey, the compressor behind the bodega, somebody's radio. The garden sat on a lot the city had sold for one dollar to a land trust after the building that stood there came down, and Ms. Popescu liked to say that nothing here was simple, that the tomatoes depended on the trust, the trust on the city, the city on taxes, the taxes on the bus garage two blocks over whose exhaust she suspected of stunting the kale. Samuel had thought this was a grandiose way to talk about vegetables until he noticed the soot on the bean leaves nearest the fence.

"Ms. Popescu," he said now, because she was filling the rain barrel by the shed, "do you know anything about the ozone thing? The hole."

She shut the tap and considered him. "I know the Montreal Protocol came up in your class. Karina mentioned it." Karina was the other side, the negative, and Samuel felt the small injustice of opponents getting there first. "I'm not telling you what to say. You'll figure out what you think."

That was the trouble. He did not yet know what he thought, and there was something embarrassing about being seventeen and not having a position. His father, who drove for a delivery company and had opinions on everything, said the whole climate argument was a scam run by people who wanted to feel important. His civics teacher said the opposite in a way that sounded rehearsed. Samuel had begun to suspect that both of them liked their positions more than the evidence, that they valorized the feeling of being right over the slower work of finding out, and he did not want to be like either of them.

He unfolded the page while Tyrell thinned the carrot seedlings. The paragraph was short. The 1987 Montreal Protocol phased out chemicals that destroyed ozone, and it was the first treaty in United Nations history to be ratified by every UN member state. He read it twice, then a third time, and sat back on his heels in the dirt.

"Every single one," he said.

"Every single one what?" Tyrell had a carrot seedling in each hand and was choosing between them.

"Every country in the UN ratified it. It's the first treaty that ever happened. In UN history." He held the page out. Tyrell wiped his hands on his knees and took it, and read, and his face did the thing faces do when an argument dies quietly.

"Well," Tyrell said. "So we lose."

"No." Samuel was surprised by how certain his own voice sounded, because he did not feel certain. "So we're wrong. It's not the same thing." He thought of Ms. Popescu's soot-covered kale, of the dollar the city had charged for the lot, of the fact that the garden existed because a dozen systems had leaned on each other and somehow not fallen over. Maybe countries were like that too. Maybe agreement was possible and just rare, like the rain barrel filling, and rarity was not the same as impossibility. But the affirmative could still be argued in a narrower way, he realized, the way a lawyer argues: not never in all of history, but not now, not fast enough, not for the harder problem with the cost spread differently. He said this out loud, slowly, watching Tyrell's face to see whether it held together.

"That's kind of a dodge," Tyrell said, but he was grinning, because dodging that you admit to is just strategy. "We lead with their treaty, we concede it, then we say one swallow isn't summer."

"One swallow," Samuel repeated. It was from somewhere, a book his grandmother had, and it fit better than anything he'd found on Saturday. He laughed, and planted a seed potato too deep, and had to dig it back out and set it again at the depth Ms. Popescu had shown him, two inches, eyes up. There was a coolness in the soil that stayed on his fingers.

On Monday the debate went the way debates go: Karina was better prepared and won on points, and afterward she said "you conceded the Protocol before I even brought it up, that was smart or crazy," and Samuel still wasn't sure which it had been. He walked home past the bus garage, past the garden, where the fence gate was open and Ms. Popescu was out there alone in the late light, pinching suckers off the tomatoes. He stopped at the fence and told her the result, and she said, "And?" and he stood there a moment with his hands in his pockets, deciding.

"I think both things are true," he said. "They agreed once, completely, and I don't know if they will again. I argued the one I could argue." He looked at the tomato rows, dark green and staked and leaning slightly toward the street. "Can I take some kale home? The leaves by the fence need washing, she said, but they're fine underneath."
